speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member marked this question with a star, indicating that he wished to have a verbal answer. The first part of the question reads:
1.	When will the second world war book of remembrance be completed?
The answer is that the contracting artist expects that the preparation of the pages of the world war II book of remembrance will be completed in or about June, 1956. The binding of the pages however, to be suitable and satisfactory, will take approximately a further period of three months.
The second part of the question reads:
Where will it be placed?
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to direction by the cabinet, a committee was established to advise the Minister of Veterans Affairs with respect to the choice of a suitable repository for the world war II book of remembrance. This committee is composed of representatives of the Department of Veterans Affairs, Department of National Defence, Department of Public Works, the federal district commission and representatives of the Canadian Legion of the British Empire Service League and of the National Council of Veterans Associations in Canada, together with the contracting artist. When this committee reports to the minister, the matter will be submitted to the cabinet.
The third part of the question reads:
Will the government give consideration to the erection of a national cenotaph to honour the fallen of all wars in which Canada has participated?
The answer is that this matter is still under consideration by the cabinet.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. Hugues Lapointe (Acting Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
maintopic: OUTBREAK AMONG CONVICTS AT PRINCE ALBERT, SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
Yesterday the hon. member for Prince Albert asked if I could report on the disturbance that broke out at the Prince Albert penitentiary. I undertook to try to have some information available today, and while I have not a completely detailed report on the matter I shall be pleased to pass on the information which has been made available to me.
The information is to the effect that a disturbance broke out in the Saskatchewan penitentiary at Prince Albert on Tuesday evening, July 12, as the inmates were being returned to their cells at the conclusion of the evening exercise period at about seven p.m. Groups totalling some 100 inmates broke away from their guards and forced their way into several of the shop buildings where considerable damage was done to the machinery and equipment. The stable and a storage building were destroyed by fire and considerable damage was done to other shop buildings by fire, including the buildings used for the vocational training of inmates. Damage was also done to supplies of foodstuffs. The rioting inmates were brought under control within an hour or so of the outbreak of the disturbance, and by nine o'clock all were locked in their cells. No inmate was injured but one guard sustained a fractured arm.
An estimate of the monetary loss sustained in this outbreak is not yet available. Inspection and appraisal of the damages is being carried out by the officers of the institution and will be available later. Arrangements have been made for one of the deputy commissioners to proceed by air to Prince Albert to investigate the circumstances of this outbreak and/ to prepare a report.
From information at present available, the cause of the outbreak is not known. No serious complaints had been received by the warden and no grievances of a serious nature had been put forward by the inmates or their committee. The institution was visited by the commissioner of penitentiaries in May of this year and at that time there was no evidence of unusual tension or serious complaints.
The hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) also suggested that there might have been a condition of overcrowding in the penitentiary. I am informed that the present population of the penitentiary is 630,


and there is accommodation available in cells and dormitories for 660 inmates, as well as hospital and dissociation cells. There is therefore ample accommodation available for the present population.
While the population of the penitentiary has been increasing steadily over the past year there has been no indication that the situation had become a serious or dangerous one owing to overcrowding.

maintopic: OUTBREAK AMONG CONVICTS AT PRINCE ALBERT, SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: May I ask a supplementary question. During the last year has any complaint been made that there was a danger through the increase in the number of prisoners over the normal number? Second, in order to clarify the situation and to remove any question of responsibility from the warden or the staff, who are an efficient group, and in order to get at the story properly, would the minister give consideration to having a judicial investigation? There are available district court judges in Saskatchewan trained in the criminal law who would be available for that purpose.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
maintopic: OUTBREAK AMONG CONVICTS AT PRINCE ALBERT, SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
I am not in a position to say whether there would have been any complaint such as my hon. friend has mentioned. However, I am informed by the authorities of the department that at no time have they considered the situation dangerous because of overcrowding.
With regard to the second part of my hon. friend's question, as I just pointed out, one of the deputy commissioners is being flown to Prince Albert to investigate the situation on the spot, and any future development I should think would be as a result of his report.
Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime
Minister): Mr. Speaker, may I add just a word so that the house will know what the situation is. There have been representations from the officers responsible for the administration of the penitentiaries that there was a constant increase in the population of places of detention, and that it was high time to commence to prepare for more adequate housing. The decision in that respect was made some months ago, and the preparatory work is under way for the establishment of,
I am not sure whether it is two or three, additional institutions so that the unfortunates who are condemned to sojourn in the penitentiaries may be more adequately provided for, and so that there may be less occasion for the kind of irritation due to crowding that sometimes breaks out, such as happened in Saskatchewan.

maintopic: OUTBREAK AMONG CONVICTS AT PRINCE ALBERT, SASKATCHEWAN

maintopic: OUTBREAK AMONG CONVICTS AT PRINCE ALBERT, SASKATCHEWAN

I think the hon. member will agree that the commissioner has been doing an excellent job in handling the penitentiaries.

maintopic: OUTBREAK AMONG CONVICTS AT PRINCE ALBERT, SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: May I ask a supplementary question on the same basis? Is the same consideration being given to the situation in the New Westminster penitentiary and in Kingston?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: OUTBREAK AMONG CONVICTS AT PRINCE ALBERT, SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: The whole system of penitentiaries throughout the whole country is being examined and reported upon, because, as the hon. member knows, it is possible, when there is space available in one province and there is requirement for that space for prisoners condemned in another province, to move them about. That requires us to keep the whole system adequate for the requirements of the whole Canadian people generally.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: We are dealing with resolution No. 236, Department of National Defence, Royal Canadian Air Force, search and rescue.

Mr. Chairman, as you will recall, I raised some matters in connection with search and rescue under the first item of the minister's estimates. At that time it was suggested that we might defer any discussion of the matter until we came to this particular heading. Perhaps I should indicate that my reason for raising the matter under this heading arises partly at least out of some discussion which took place at the last session on the subject of the coastguard service for Canada, and in particular for the west coast of British Columbia.
At that time the then minister of transport, Mr. Chevrier, suggested that in effect a satisfactory substitute for such a coastguard service was being provided by the search and rescue under the R.C.A.F. At that time I was willing to accept the suggestion temporarily that if a satisfactory substitute were being provided I would be prepared to go along with the idea that we should not create an entirely new organization with the overhead that would be entailed and the additional expenses to the taxpayer that would be involved. As a result, though, I did make a particular point during the time between last session and this session to observe, where it was possible for me to do so, the actual working out of the arrangement under search and rescue. I was able to observe that a number of boats were tied in with this plan,

Supply-National Defence namely, the boats under the operation of our Department of Fisheries. The lifeboat stations at Bamfield and Tofino operated under the Department of Transport and also boats operated by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. However, I must say that all of these particular boats, as I have observed them, are certainly not very substantial craft. The patrol vessels of our Department of Fisheries may be quite adequate for the patrol duties of the department but, as far as my observation goes and according to information given to me, they are not designed to deal with the serious matter of rescue operations in bad weather on our open Pacific waters.
During a trip from Sidney to Anacortes through the San Juan islands, which, as members realize, are in the United States, I noticed a very sleek and substantial vessel lying in one of the harbours of those islands, which are in inside sheltered waters. It was a vessel that appeared to me to be much more adequate for sea rescue work than any of the vessels that I had seen operated under the various departments I have mentioned. This vessel was sitting there very much as a fire truck sits in a fire hall, apparently ready to go at a moment's notice, if called upon to participate in rescue work.
I am not raising this to criticize the value of the aerial patrol and the co-ordination work which may be undertaken under the R.C.A.F. I know also that they operate at least a couple of small crash boats on the eastern coast of Vancouver island which are tied in with the search and rescue operations. But, as far as I know, apart from the two lifeboat stations at Bamfield and Tofino, there is nothing on the west coast that is directly equivalent to the U.S. coastguard service.
I was pleased to be able to secure the information from the Minister of Justice, when the estimates of the R.C.M.P. were under consideration, that a larger vessel is* to be put into service for the west coast of Vancouver island detachment of the R.C.M.P. As far as I can judge from the information he gave us, it is a more adequate type of vessel to be on call for rescue work in the waters of the Pacific, which certainly are not always peaceful.
In the white paper, reference is made on page 10, under paragraph 35, to search and rescue, and I am going to quote some parts of that paragraph which I think are relevant particularly to what I have in mind. It says:
Although elements of each of the armed forces, the R.C.M.P. and other government departments may be called on to assist in search and rescue operations, the R.C.A.F. ... is responsible for

the co-ordination and supervision of search and rescue activities and for the provision of certain minimum facilities in Canada.
I am confining any remarks I make entirely to the west coast, because I do not know anything of what the situation may be on the Atlantic coast or, for that matter, in the great lakes. That can be brought forward by members from those areas, if they so desire. But one thing which interests me is the mention that elements from each of the armed forces are involved in this. In particular I am interested in knowing what form of participation in search and rescue under direction of the Royal Canadian Air Force is given by the Royal Canadian Navy.
I also notice in the white paper a table is given on page 7 showing the strength of the fleet as at December 31, 1954. I am not too familiar with just what types of vessels are described there. I notice, for example, that there are 10 destroyer escorts in commission and 14 under construction. I notice there are eight coastal minesweepers in commission and six under construction. I assume that some of those vessels are attached to the naval station at Esquimalt, which is suggested also on page 7 of the white paper, as being one of the two principal commands of the navy.
I know that periodically one does see vessels of the Royal Canadian Navy up the western coast of Vancouver island. Usually they are paying what is publicized as a courtesy visit to such ports as Port Alberni, but one of the questions that arise in my mind in this connection is this. If these vessels are going to be in operation on the west coast and are going to be engaged, as I assume, in various training duties, could they not be utilized to a greater extent, at least, than I have observed them as having been used, in the search and rescue operations? I wonder, for example, why it would not be possible to have one or two of the smaller naval vessels stationed at a substation, let us say at Quatsino sound in the northern part of Vancouver island, or possibly located in the Queen Charlottes, so that they would be more immediately on call if required for rescue operations than they appear to be now.
I hope the minister, as he suggested he would do when we were discussing this matter on the first item, will be prepared to give some statement based on the questions I have raised. As far as I am concerned, I am prepared to be convinced that the search and rescue operation is a satisfactory substitute for a coastguard, but from what I have been able to observe so far, I am not convinced that that is the case. I am not

concerned particularly about my personal satisfaction in this matter; but, if it could be demonstrated to the satisfaction of the people who are directly concerned with this problem on our coasts that a satisfactory substitute for a coastguard service can be provided at a smaller cost than would be involved in creating a Canadian equivalent of the U.S. coastguard, that is something which could be accepted. But I know I am not alone when I say that many of the people on the west coast of British Columbia are not convinced that that is the case. I hope the minister may be able to give some further clarification of how this service operates and, in particular, some details as to how these other elements of the armed forces co-operate with the air force under this heading.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as the hon. member is well aware, the coastline of British Columbia is of very great length. What he appears to be suggesting would be very extensive. In the second place, any system of search and rescue involves primarily a matter of time. Search and rescue problems must be met quickly. There is a disability of a coastguard system that I think Is met by the search and rescue elements co-ordinated by the air force, and that is the question of time. If an accident occurs or if distress signals are received, there is always the question of time in arriving at the scene of the trouble. That is why the search and rescue division of the air force has been put in charge of such operations in this sense.
The mounted police and the Department of Transport have vessels on the coast. There are a great number of tugs on the coast, and they all have wireless. There are a substantial number of naval vessels on the coast also and they travel up and down the coast on exercises. So far as British Columbia is concerned all these elements are tied in to the search and rescue centre of the air force on Sea island. We have there a search and rescue squadron with paratroop doctors and nurses and persons especially trained for these duties.
Taken altogether, I think the operation is a successful one because when any trouble is reported, whether it is at sea or on land-* and this is the same procedure that is followed throughout Canada-the search and rescue squadron is the focal point where all these calls are dealt with. They on their part are familiar with movements of ships, naval movements and tug boat movements and are in a position to quickly get in touch with any useful unit such as ships or vessels near the scene of the accident. In addition,
Supply-National Defence if there is no vessel nearby, they can themselves fly there in the shortest possible time. This system has worked out well.
I notice that in 1954-and these figures are for all Canada-the Royal Canadian Air Force search and rescue units flew 2,720 hours. That shows that they were busily engaged. They dealt with 230 cases involving flying, 34 of which were from aircraft distress, 40 of which were marine distress calls, and 119 were mercy flights. There were 37 other miscellaneous cases.
I believe the system of search and rescue involving all these elements that I have mentioned, centring on the search and rescue unit of the Royal Canadian Air Force, provides an excellent service and provides it quickly and at a much less cost. In that way we get the co-operation of tugboats, and of naval vessels along the coast, and we utilize all these elements by means of radio to the best advantage at any given time.

I quite appreciate some of the things the minister has said, and there is one particular thing he mentioned which I agree is of the essence. That is the matter of time. The thing that concerns me is this. What guarantee is there that there is going to be a boat available within any reasonable distance if an emergency arises? For example, the minister mentioned that tugboats are tied in with this system. I was aware of that fact. But what guarantee is there that there is going to be a tugboat somewhere out on the northwest coast of Vancouver island at the time that a distressing situation arises? As far as I am concerned, that is the crux of the matter.
The vessels operated by the Department of Fisheries or by the R.C.M.P. up until the present time, or the motorized lifeboat type of boats which are used at the lifeboat stations at Bamfield and Tofino, are the only ones which are on call within a defined area. According to my observations and according to the comments that have been made to me by people who are much more familiar than I am with the details of seafaring, those boats are not really adequate to deal with situations that may arise.
That is one of the reasons I have raised this question as to whether or not, at relatively small expense, some elements of the navy's vessels could be stationed-I pick examples at random-at Quatsino sound, which is near the northern end of Vancouver island, or in the Queen Charlotte islands. Is there any assurance that adequate services of rescue vessels are going to be available when needed?

Supply-National Defence

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member, who knows the Pacific coast as well as I do, knows that there are a vast number of tugs and small vessels all along the coast all the time. Naval vessels are also doing exercises up and down the coast. If the search and rescue operations were left to a coastguard in the accepted sense of that term, they could not begin to have anything like the number of ships distributed as are now distributed up and down the British Columbia coast. All of these vessels, incidentally, can be reached from Sea island at any time. But if, in fact, an accident occurs and there are no vessels within quick reach of the scene of the accident, the search and rescue unit itself has Cansos, which can reach almost any part of the coast quickly.
I therefore think the situation is covered better by the present system, with the correlation of all the elements which can be used, than it would be covered if we had a substantial number, if you like, at great cost, of coastguard vessels spotted along the coast. I think the present system, in addition to being much cheaper, covers the area much better and is more effective.

I note the minister said the air force was involved in 34 incidents of lost aircraft. Is there any arrangement for reimbursing the government for any cost of this service or is this total borne by the air force?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I understand that the disposition of aircraft in the search and rescue picture is in accordance with the practice of the international organization called ICAO. We have certain areas for which we are responsible. We are not paid by the international organization for utilizing our services in that regard. We stand the cost ourselves.

I might say to the minister that I think the air force deserves a great deal of credit for the work that is being carried out. I understand that prior to this type of organization, it was a rather loosely knit affair when we came to do a job of this kind. I have heard one criticism that I think should be passed along. In the far northern areas I think the force does, and maybe with some reason, stick to a very firm plan as far as search is concerned. It works on a grid system and follows a very firm pattern. I have heard the criticism that at times those in charge do not take into account the special knowledge possessed by the far north operators with respect to whether a flyer involved in a forced landing might have taken advantage of the cover provided by certain surroundings and things like that if he was in distress. I strongly


suggest that word be passed along that if there are special conditions of that kind the search master should pay special attention to them because I feel it might cut down a great deal on the time and expense involved in an operation of this kind.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Then search and rescue is carried. Defence research and development is carried. Then we come to mutual aid.

I notice there is a reduction in this item which is chiefly due to reduced commitments as far as the supply of aircraft and other materials are concerned. Would the minister say a word in explanation? I presume the reduction is brought about by the fact that the requirements have been met to a great extent and therefore the commitments in the year ahead are not so great.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think the situation is that when mutual aid was instituted the other countries of NATO in Europe were not in a good position to provide with any degree of speed much of the equipment necessary to reorganize their forces. At that time our service had considerable surpluses of equipment from world war II. There were also certain types which we were replacing. Thus in the early stages of rearmament in Europe mutual aid was founded on the basis of giving the maximum help in respect of those things which we could most usefully give. As the defence production industry developed in Canada we extended mutual aid to include some of that production. To help keep our plants running and to aid in our own rearmament we made contributions from time to time of various elements being made in Canada, among them airplanes.
The mutual aid program has been going on now since 1950, and in the meantime the build-up of forces in Europe has grown. Their production industries for defence purposes have grown. As time goes on and our allies develop their own armed forces and the means of sustaining them I would assume that mutual aid would continue to shrink. There are certain elements of mutual aid that will of course continue. For example, the air training scheme, which is quite expensive, will go on until 1957. In the second place, Canada is now undertaking changes in emphasis in our own defence program, a large element of which consists of radar lines, such as the mid-Canada line, which is just as much an element in NATO defence as in the defence of Canada and the United States. Therefore as our commitments for continental defence grow, and because there are large numbers of spares we intend to provide for what we have already given away, I think the common-sense thing to do is not to increase mutual aid but rather

to reduce it gradually. What we are trying to do is tie ourselves into the NATO picture in the most useful way and at the same time to keep our defence commitments within the bounds of what we can hope to raise financially.
It is a fact though that the reduction of $136 million in the total defence budget is accounted for to the extent of $125 million by the reduction in mutual aid.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes.

I notice that the contribution to infrastructure and NATO budgets has increased from $19 million to $25 million. I have no criticism to make of the increase, but perhaps the minister might explain how the contributions to infrastructure are allocated and spent. I am thinking particularly of the standards which must be met in the construction of areodromes and buildings of that sort. I understand that the standards vary from country to country. Is it the case that there are over-all standards set by NATO and that the variation, if any, is accounted for merely by the standard of workmanship or is there a variation in standards from one country to another? Do the countries themselves have control over the standards with respect to buildings constructed in the particular country?
This question arises in my mind because of reports-I do not know whether or not they are justified but the minister can clear up the matter-that there is quite a variation in the standard of accommodation for our air force squadrons in Europe, depending on the country in which they happen to be. I do not want to make any odious comparisons, but I understand that most personnel would prefer the standard of accommodation provided in one country rather than that provided in another.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I might make two observations. The hon. member has referred to the different standards of aerodromes in Europe. That was the case before 1949, but I am informed that the NATO council officials have now fixed minimum standards for all aerodromes within the NATO area. If any nation using these aerodromes wishes supplementary facilities they have to provide them, but there is a standard now which I think is reasonably acceptable. With respect to the difference so far as housing for personnel is concerned, housing is the responsibility of the country supplying the forces. We make arrangements or have made arrangements in both France and Germany in that regard.
Then, the hon. member made a comment about the increase in the estimates for the
Supply-National Defence cost of the infrastructure and the NATO budget. The reason for that change is that up until this year part of those charges came from other government funds. This year, we are following the same practice as the United States and placing all the infrastructure expenses and the NATO contributions under the mutual aid program.

I have two further brief questions. One is as to the provision of married quarters for dependents of Canadian personnel in Europe. Has that commitment been completely met now, as well as the provision of schools? The second part of my question is, what provision is made for the rapid evacuation of dependents of Canadian personnel from Europe if such a thing should suddenly become necessary?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I understand that the married quarters required by our forces in Germany, both the army and the air force, are completed and practically all occupied. Some of the married quarters in France are finished and occupied, while others are still in the process of completion. The same thing applies in each country with respect to schools; a certain number have been completed while others are still being completed.
I do not know that I would care to enter into a discussion as to the evacuation of dependents, other than to assure the hon. member that this subject is under discussion with our NATO allies because it is naturally a very real problem. I think we would prefer not to give any information about the methods and plans which are being evolved.
Can the minister give a target date as to when it is hoped that complete accommodation will be provided for married dependents in France?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Midsummer next year has always been the target for our program and we think we will attain it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The discussion on mutual aid has been completed and that completes the items under resolution 236, but I understand that the committee agreed to provide an opportunity for the discussion of publications. Shall I call that heading now?

As I said last night, Mr. Chairman, there is nothing that could possibly induce me to inflict myself at any great length on the members of the committee at this late stage except a matter of very great importance. I do not know whether all other hon. members of the committee feel that this is a matter of great importance, but in the light of what I have experienced and what was said last night by the hon. member for

Supply-National Defence Lethbridge, I feel it would be desirable for me to make a statement this morning.
At the outset may I say that the minister very kindly sent to my office a number of copies of the Current Affairs publication about which the hon. member for Lethbridge spoke last night. He sent me all of those beginning with January of this year up to the present time. I have had a chance to do some homework, and I thought that I should like to present a balanced statement, as fair a statement as I possibly could, because what was said by the hon. member for Lethbridge last night I am sure must have raised considerable doubt in the minds of some people. I do want to try to set them straight, and if possible give the members of the committee the benefit of whatever research I may have been able to conduct.
May I tell you first, Mr. Chairman, why it was that I became interested in these publications. I have four boys. One of them is a 20-year-old attending Queen's University school of medicine. He frequently comes home during his school year, and this young man is quite typical of the thousands of young men who are in the armed services, and I would think about on an average with them in his mentality and ability. One time during this past winter he came home, and in the course of our discussion, such as father and son do have, he told me about a discussion he had had the day before with a young officer from the staff training college in Kingston. Now, this was just about the substance of that talk. It turned on what goes on in college. The young officer told my son about the visiting lecturers, and how the lectures are conducted. Then he said to my lad, "When I get through listening to the lectures I am left with a definite impression that a communist victory in the present great world struggle is inevitable. 1 hear so much about how clever the communists are and how dumb and stupid the democracies are, and that seems to be played up." I said to the lad, "Well, what effect does that have on your mind, and what effect do you think it would have on many young people in the services throughout Canada or the world, for that matter?" The reply I got was this: It must have left them with a feeling of futility, a feeling of what is the use of fighting against communism if it is inevitable that communism is going to prevail.
My interest was aroused as a consequence of that discussion. When my attention was drawn to the publication Current Affairs- by the way, I have known of it for some years, but these particular ones about which the hon. member for Lethbridge complained


last night were put into my hands and I read some of them. I went through all of them rather carefully. As I read them I wondered just what effect they would have upon the mind of a 20-year-old in the armed services, who was away from home and being, educated, informed or indoctrinated by the kind of thing we find in these Current Affairs publications.
Let me explain just briefly to the committee what they are. These Current Affairs publications are little booklets that are issued bi-monthly by the information service of the Department of National Defence. They are supposed to be accompanied by discussion leaflets and, so far as I can gather, they are supposed to be placed in the hands of skilled leaders in discussion to be used as a foundation for discussion. But they are also placed in the hands of members of the services, old or young, and they are read quite widely. Some of them are written by prominent writers. For instance, I see one in this compilation, volumes 1 and 2 for 1951-52, written by Blair Fraser, a very prominent editorial writer and newspaperman. I see another one here written by Charles J. Woodsworth, and so on, all very prominent writers on all kinds of subjects.
Let me say right off, Mr. Chairman, that I have gone through these publications as carefully as I possibly could. Let me say that in the main the articles contained in these publications are objective and fairly factual, and I find nothing very objectionable in them. But aside from one I must say that, in this whole lot, beginning with October 1951 and ending with June 1952, I never found one single inspirational article-not one. There was one that bordered a bit on the inspirational, written by a Jesuit priest. But, aside from that, there was not the semblance of an approach to anything that could be classed as inspirational.
But there was in it-and I think this is what the hon. member for Lethbridge was complaining about last night, more than anything else-an article written by Charles Woodsworth called "Threat in the East". It made up the whole of the pamphlet for November 15, 1951. The hon. member for Lethbridge described these things, and I suppose that under normal circumstances he would have quoted them last night. I would have, if I had had them in hand at the time. Here is the way Mr. Woodsworth starts:
In Asia as throughout the world, a desperate struggle is going on for men's minds. It is a struggle between liberal forces, trying to bring freedom, enlightenment, and social justice to mankind, and forces suppressing individual liberty and employing the methods of the totalitarian police state.

He does not identify them at all. He starts right off, and leaves it to these young men to conjecture. He leaves it to them to decide for themselves which are the liberal forces which are trying to bring freedom, enlightenment and social justice to mankind, and those forces which are suppressing individual liberty and employing the methods of the totalitarian state. Then he goes on to say:
Who, or what, is the adversary of this freedom that is the aim of liberalism and social justice?
And he leaves it dangling there, so that anyone is left wondering whether it is the communist world or the capitalist world, or what it is. He does not attempt to answer; but he goes on to say this:
Basically the trouble lies in the wretched conditions under which millions of people exist today; conditions' of poverty, ill-health, ignorance, illiteracy; conditions bordering on starvation and devoid of all sense of security.
He does not answer the question at all. He leaves it to these boys to wonder; and many of them would be very likely to come to the conclusion that the liberal forces trying to bring freedom, enlightenment and social justice to mankind would be the communist forces. That is what any normal boy would assume, as a consequence of reading that. Then, a little later on, in the same pamphlet Mr. Woodsworth says at page 6:
Every member of the communist party in the various countries of the world, whether he understands it or not, is working in the interest of the Soviet government. The effect of this is that in practice Russia is always right and the end justifies the means.
I have quoted that paragraph, without taking it out of its context. It is right there. "What would any bright young man deduce from that, except that here is something that so many people of the world think is worth while, that each of them is actually ready to die for his convictions, and that there is not much use fighting against this sort of thing, because it is really doing things for people.
I quote from the same publication at page 11, where Mr. Woodsworth says:
In its origins Chinese communism depended on the desperate desire of millions of Chinese peasants for a fairer, more equal division of land, and some form of administration which would give it to them and guarantee that they could keep the fruits of their labour.
And he leaves it at that; he leaves it to the boy to conclude, "Well, communism has done it; communism is the answer; therefore communism is the thing we ought to be looking into because it will divide the land fairly and set up a government which would administer it." That is the kind of thing about which the hon. member for Lethbridge was complaining last night; that is
Supply-National Defence the kind of thing which indoctrinates these young minds and makes them feel, "What is the use of our putting up a fight against communism, when it does such wonderful things and inspires people to such wonderful ideals?"
That is the important point; and the hon. member for Lethbridge was on sound ground when he stepped on that sort of thing. And in what I am saying I am sorry to have to include my friend Blair Fraser. He was asked to write one of these articles, headed "The Threat from Communism", and it was published on October 15, 1951. Anyone can read it. I shall not delay the committee by reading it or quoting from it, but I recommend it to hon. members for purposes of reading. And when an hon. member has read it he might ask himself: What would a 20-year-old make of that? I would say that when a 20-year-old got through reading that he could come to only one conclusion, and that would be the utter futility of attempting to fight against this tremendous power that is sweeping the world and is bound to win.
That sort of thing it seems to me is poor stuff to put in the hands of young men in the army, young men who need to be inspired and whose faith needs to be built up, young men who need to be released from the grip of fear. I invite hon. members to read the article and make up their minds with regard to it. I am not for one moment trying to exaggerate.
Now let me come to more recent times. The hon. member for Lethbridge quoted from this group of publications from back in 1951 and 1952. As I said earlier, very kindly the minister sent me all this year's publications. He did not make any special selection-he just took the whole group and sent them to me. Well, I did some homework on them and, for the first time in my reading of these publications, I found something inspirational. I commend the minister, because it indicates what I have felt since I have read those published from January 1 to July 2 of this year. I believe I detected a change, and I commend the minister-because I am sure there is a change, and that it is a change for the better.
In only one article have I found something to complain about, and I shall reveal it in a moment. I cannot expect the minister constantly to be poring over these manuscripts, because men have been selected in his department to do that, to edit them carefully and to see that nothing gets out and into the hands of these young men that would destroy their faith.

Supply-National Defence
I would refer particularly to this one of April 15. I find in it an excellent article on "Vital Ground for Democracy", but the article is not signed. I do not know who wrote it. Since the new minister came to office I have discovered fewer publications signed with the names of prominent writers than one found before. This may be a change in policy and, if so, perhaps it is a change for the better. However, I was about to point out that in this article I found the first approach to a spiritual balance to be found anywhere in these publications. This augurs well, and my mind is set at rest to some considerable degree when I find this happening.
I would quote particularly from pages 22 and 23 of the article to show its truly inspirational nature. It develops something that the boy should have and should understand. It gives them a real reason for rising to defend their way of life. That is the kind of thing I like to see, and it is the kind of thing I believe the young men should have; but I am sorry to have to criticize another one. This one is the March, 1955 issue, and it is headed: "In the U.S.S.R.". For the life of me, Mr. Chairman, I cannot understand why we should have to go to great lengths and expense to publish a booklet of this kind called "In the U.S.S.R." and give it to our boys, especially when it tends to glorify what is going on in the U.S.S.R. I do not mind, in fact I think we have to be balanced in our judgment in these things-it will not do the boys any harm to know. I think they have to know both sides of the question. The thing that bothers me, Mr. Chairman, is that in this issue, "In the U.S.S.R." you find the following. I am reading from page 4, which is the very beginning of the article. Listen to this:
Let us picture the almost entirely agricultural Canada of 1900 trying to become a great industrial power overnight-a Canada seeking to multiply its Ungavas, Arvidas, Kitimats, International Nickels and Leducs in a hurry instead of filling the stores of Montreal, Toronto, or Vancouver. To carry out such a program there must be a thorough levelling, centralization and regimentation of the whole country, its capital resources and its people, sealing the frontiers so that the inhabitants will not know and consequently cannot envy the material prosperity abroad, sealing the frontiers to prevent emigration and keep the workers at home, sealing the frontiers above all against competition.
They are just throwing it at the boys the first minute they get hold of the book I continue:
Assuming that the people are agricultural, a proportion must be transformed into city dwellers and labourers, and staffs of engineers and technicians must be created.
And so on. He goes on to say what must be done, and at the very best it can be only a rank apology for what the U.S.S.R. has


done. In not one single sentence does it say what terrible things they did in order to build up their present strength. Listen to this on page 6:
The five-year plans came in 1928 in the guise of a regular mobilization, first of hammers and sickles, then of turbines and tractors. This picture is no exaggeration if we remember the fight against the kulaks, great farmers who sought to defend their property and were brought to heel only by detachments of the party, the army and the police. Many of them died in the struggle. The rest were sent to people Siberia.
If I ever heard of a deliberate misrepresentation of fact, Mr. Chairman, this is it. It refers to the kulaks. Many thousands of them were ruthlessly destroyed because they would not give up what they owned at the moment. The article says: "In the struggle many of them died." Bless my soul, our boys have been handed that sort of tripe and we expect them to be prepared to fight, to defend our way of life, in the light of that kind of apology. I do not blame the minister for this one. I cannot expect him to be able to go through every manuscript and to see that it is properly written. We have to be fair about it. In fairness, I must say, Mr. Chairman, that this issue published on March 1, 1955, is the only one published this year to which I take any exception whatsoever, and I commend the minister for that. I do believe the minister needs more help. I certainly would suggest that he allow the members of the House of Commons to help him. It might be wise to put the members on the mailing list and let them get these pamphlets, and they will be glad to help the minister.
If I had obtained this issue early enough, I would have gone to the minister and brought to his attention what is in it, and perhaps we might have prevented its getting into the hands of young men with immature minds, many of them with untrained minds, who would be bowled over by this kind of propaganda. May I just leave that for the moment?
The question is, are we or are we not designing the information services, these that I am speaking about and others in the government, so that they become a real inspiration to our young men in the armed forces, or are they of a character which destroys the will to resist evil forces, that destroys faith and makes the boys victims of fear? My criticism of all of the pamphlets that I have seen is as much of what they do not contain as of what they do contain. It would be wise for us all to be much more vigilant.
I have gone through these pamphlets, and I should like to say a few things, if I may.
I do not want to take too much time, but I think it is vital to say a few things about

what they do not contain, and what I believe fighting forces of a country as great and as prosperous and with as great a future as Canada should have if they are going to have the will to stand up and defend it.
As I have said, I have four boys. I would want every single one of those boys to prepare himself to defend his country and I would do my very best to stand with them under all circumstances, but I would want them to have the faith and the will, the background, the knowledge and the information that would lead them to be worthy representatives, and to stand up for their country, its institutions and our way of life. There is little or nothing in these pamphlets that says anything about the awful things that have been done by the communist imperialists and in the name of communism. They should know that.
There is very little in any of these pamphlets, Mr. Chairman, that speaks of the superiority of the free way of life. I find, too, that there is only a tiny reference here and there to the communists taking over various free places and the methods by which it was done. There is little, if anything, that I find about the glorious traditions of the British Empire and the tremendous value of the gifts and contributions to the whole world made by Britain and her associated countries of the commonwealth. I have not been able to find in my search very much, if anything, about the need for recognizing the spiritual nature of the earth, the spiritual side of man, and that this side of man needs exercise just as much as does the physical side if he is to be balanced and full of faith in God and free from fear. I have not found very much, if anything, in them about that. I have not found anything in them except the one that I mentioned this morning, the one that was issued at the end of April this year celebrating Easter month, that man was created a free moral agent, and that he is entitled to remain free from religious and political compulsions that may be considered as unrighteous dominion being exercised by men through the power they have been able to accumulate in their hands, the wherewithal to exercise that unrighteous dominion. I have not been able to find that. I find in no single publication in this information service thus far any real effort to inspire faith and courage to meet what is ahead. I have always in my days, Mr. Chairman, found a great many things of an inspirational nature in the story of the Bible, the things that are said there that are real history to me. When I was going through these things I wondered whether I could find anything that approaches the account of how Gideon in ancient times saved Israel from the Midianite threat at
Supply-National Defence Mount Gilboa, the inspiring story of how God stood by men in those days when they were on the side of righteousness. I have not found anything of that kind, but I did find there is too much inclination to play down the Bible as an old maid's tale, to cast reflection on it and not give it the credence that it deserves.
I find, for instance, most people tell us we cannot use these things from the Bible because the Bible is no longer accepted as true. As a matter of fact, they point out that we should remember that one part of the strategy of militant materialism, that is Godless communism, both of the communist and fascist types, by the way, is to undermine and destroy faith in the Bible as the history of God's dealings with men in times past.
I visited Israel last year and had a good chance to look around. In the course of my looking around I ran across some things that aroused my admiration and keen interest. I discovered, for example, that archaeological expeditions had been in there for years, some as far back as 1914 or 1915. Of those archaeological expeditions from all over the world, perhaps the first of any note was that led by Sir Charles Marston. Using the Bible as their guide, those expeditions were able to discover the ruins and remnants of some of the ancient city states.
I have in mind particularly one that is now the site of great concentration camps where there are about 80,000 to 100,000 Arab refugees from Israel, the ancient city of Jericho. Sir Charles Marston and his group went into that area and started digging into the sand dunes that had blown in and covered the remnants of the ancient city. Using the Bible as their guide, they dug down and discovered the remnants of the ancient city. The first things of any account they found there were remnants of pottery. World experts on pottery, after studying them carefully, said that they belonged to the era of approximately the time of Joshua. Then they discovered, by very carefully clearing away the sand, that it was a walled city. They discovered a most astounding thing- that there was plenty of evidence all around that the walls had fallen down, exactly as the account in the Bible says they did.
Furthermore, digging in the dunes outside the city, they discovered the burial places of the kings of the city state. One in particular that they discovered was the burial place of the king of the city state at the time of Joshua. He had on his finger the signet ring that had been given him by the rulers of Egypt, which he would use to impress into the wax sealing any proclamation or document, exactly establishing the time of the

Supply-National Defence existence of this city and proving exactly what Sir Charles Marston said, that the Bible is true and that the stories that are told in the Bible have real foundation. I could tell you more on this, but I must not do so.
May I suggest that the minister and his department ask themselves what effort is made these days in the information services to make the men in the services acquainted with the rich store of inspiring events that are to be found in the history of Britain's past and that of the commonwealth, especially events that are connected with times of great danger and times of war. I draw your attention, Mr. Chairman and Mr. Minister, to the fact that in the railway committee room of this very house is a great picture of Canadians arriving at Vimy Ridge. One sees in it supernatural beings, drawing our attention to an event in the history of the first world war wherein our forces were given unsuspected aid which was undoubtedly from spiritual sources. Are our boys being made acquainted with that inspiring event? No, they are not. I find no evidence whatever that they are.
I wonder if they have been told about the angels of Mons and other events in the first world war that they should know about. I wonder in what pamphlet or other information service are they made aware of what happened on July 4, 1942, in the desert fighting in North Africa. I refer the hon. members of this committee to a little book written by Major Peter W. Rainier, a book called "Pipeline to Battle". That tells of a marvellous event that occurred on July 4, 1942, when 1,100 of the toughest of the Panzer troops of Germany gave themselves up to an almost obliterated force of British. Here is the man who was there and saw it. Here is the man who was involved in the building of the pipeline which was one of the instruments by which this surrender came about. You know as well as I do, Mr. Chairman, that to capture a handful of Panzer troops would have been a triumph, but to have 1,100 of them surrender was something amazing. I wonder if our boys are being given that story. I should just like to quote a very short conclusion that Major Rainier wrote in his book "Pipeline to Battle". He says:
In the hours that followed, these 1,100 men suffered unspeakably. That mistake turned the tide of battle! But the question that arises in our minds is:	Why was the pipeline full of salt
water? And why just at the very moment when the Germans broke through the British lines at the point where the pipeline ran along the surface?
Major Rainier was the builder of the line. He says it was a new one, never used before. On that fateful day of the break-through it was being tested for leaks. Rainier did not want to waste precious fresh water, hence

used salt water for the test. The Germans came along at that very time at that very place and shot holes through the pipe line, sank to their knees and quickly gulped the water. Then they found themselves in a terrible state physically and gave themselves up in despair. The writer concludes as follows:
If Alamein had occurred the day before, the line would have been empty. Two days later it would have been full of fresh water. As it happened the nazis got the salt water. On so small a turn of fate is history written. Was it luck? I suggest it is well beyond the bounds of coincidence. It was God watching over Britain and saving her again by a miracle!
I wonder, Mr. Chairman, how much of that kind of information is given to our boys to inspire them. These and similar stories would really inspire the men of our forces, give them spiritual exercise and build in them a sustaining faith. I know there are some hon. members who call it time, but I have a short conclusion I should like to put on record.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member has five more minutes.

To sum up, Mr. Chairman, I find in all these information services, which I have gone through most carefully, very little or at best only a word, about the impossibility of human scheming ever being able to answer the strategy of materialism of which both the leftist-if we may call them so- and the rightist varieties are well advanced. Our boys are not being informed, for instance, that communism and fascism are the well-springs of this Godless materialism or militant atheism. They are not being shown the truth about how militant atheism stems from the complacency of the Christian forces in the face of moral evil and material oppression.
This militant atheism, about which I think they should be informed, has already gained so much ground that in my judgment it has become impossible to preach the gospel freely in many lands-the gospel that is so well known and beloved throughout the world. Even in some of the western countries it seems necessary today to devise an entirely new language to reach the working millions, a new language in which to convey the historic Christian truths which generations gone by understood so well. My father and your father stood firmly for their Christian beliefs. Why are not the boys being told these things, with adequate evidence to show that it is true? If they are to serve their country and the cause of righteousness, they must know that what they stand for is right and good.
They must have a deep and abiding faith in it. They must not be fed that kind of

thing which will destroy their faith. They must come to understand that there is an answer to communism, which is Godless materialism. That answer can only be-and it should be placed before them as often as possible-an inspired world-wide strategy which comes through Divine guidance to those who are prepared to listen to God and to remove the moral and spiritual blocks to being able to hear the word of God. Through people of this calibre I think the Holy Spirit can work effectively across the whole world and get over the message. Our boys must learn that the answer to communism and fascism and above all to this rank materialism is a hate-free, fear-free, greed-free people who have developed a firmly-rooted faith in God, in themselves, in their cause and in their institutions; I refer to Canadian institutions.
The kind of information service that I have been able to see thus far is one in which everything but the kind of thing I have talked about is to be found. In times like these I say that we need more inspiration, more of the kind of thing that will help our boys to train effectively, to be willing to use their energies to defend this country, instead of feeding them the kind of thing that will cause doubts in their minds. Mr. Chairman, may I appeal to the minister to make every effort to see that the kind of information service that goes out to these young men is the kind that will contain inspirational material, the kind of material that will help them to gain real strength through their knowledge and conviction that they are fighting for the thing that is right.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, my remarks will be brief, but I do not propose to permit the discussion of publications to which reference has already been made to pass without some comment about a significant feature of those publications. There has been some improvement. Mention has already been made of the issue in regard to the U.S.S.R. That issue should never have gone out. It is a thoroughly inaccurate portrayal of Soviet Russia. It is a highly-coloured propaganda document which completely ignores the hardships, the slavery, the cruelty and the existence of at least 12 million people in slave camps. I am going to leave it there.
But I wish that anyone would read this issue-that is the issue of March 1, 1955- under the heading "In the U.S.S.R." and compare it with any reliable, objective description of Russia today. I can compare it with the Russia I saw before the war and I know that it is so wrong in the absence of any balancing factors that no one reading this would have the opportunity to know about 50433-387
Supply-National Defence Russia. Yet in relation to that, there is a pamphlet which suggests questions and answers that might be asked. If they are going to have questions and answers, let them have an objective picture. I shall not extend my remarks. I have said here so much about communism that I do not think perhaps I can add any more to what I have already said about the evil of that system or the desirability of our people's knowing what it really is.
Since this discussion arose I have looked at recent issues of Current Affairs. I think it would be unfortunate to permit one feature of these publications to pass unnoticed. These are supposed to be publications placed before young Canadians some distance away from Canada in order to give them an objective picture of Canada. But so far as these publications are concerned, Canada is a one-party state already. Just read through these publications. It is true that there are stories under various headings, about the U.S.S.R., about the post office, about food and the people, United Nations achievements, Central America, the quiz, vital ground for democracy and many other subjects of that kind. But so far as these are concerned, we have already passed to the stage of a one-party state as far as any impression could be gained by those reading them. That is so, Mr. Chairman, with one exception that I have found.
I have found that one exception in volume 8 of June 15, 1955, and that has on the front "Review of Events". This gives a review of events in different countries with an appropriate introduction by the Minister of National Defence. I do not want to be unkind, but each volume is used as a means of making an appropriate appeal to the troops by the Minister of Natioanl Defence. That is what is called "soft selling" in advertising terms. It creates the impression of the benign interest of the Minister of National Defence and there is, of course, no other influence displayed in the same way. We have various headings in the review of events and then we come to Canada and here the only people mentioned are ministers of the crown. It is a one-party state so far as any stranger to Canada reading this publication is concerned. We must assume that this is written with the idea that it will inform people because these are the bases for quizzes. In each one of these there is a review of the discussion material and then a form of questions that may be asked. Let me just read you one item where they really get away for once from the one-party state:
Nov. 8. By-eiections in Canada resulted in the retention of five seats by the Liberals and the loss of one which the C.C.F. gained.

Mr. Chairman, whoever wrote that paragraph had not heard of York West where the Conservative candidate substantially increased the majority of the previous member. Nor did they hear anything about Stormont where a large majority by the previous minister who was translated to another occupation was almost changed to a victory for the Conservative party. No, Mr. Chairman; there were six by-elections. Four of those where there had been a large Liberal majority were retained, one was lost to the C.C.F. and one held by the Conservative party was retained by the hon. member for York West who has been giving distinguished representation to the riding since he came into the House of Commons. But that was the only case where the one-party state myth was dinted and the C.C.F. did slip in there. I compliment them on that achievement. They did that because they gained that seat from the Liberals. It was the Liberals, of course, who were the only important subject of discussion in this memorandum.
Mr. Chairman, this is not without its importance. Here we have one of the numerous examples of money being spent by this government in the guise of information which is straight propaganda.
Liberal propaganda.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
And straight Liberal propaganda. It would be impossible to place before this committee all the cases where that has happened. But let this leave no uncertainty in the minds of hon. members of the House of Commons or of the public of the very real attempt that is being made by this government to work toward a one-party state through their propaganda methods and in ways of which we cannot be aware. We have had a recent debate that indicated the secret methods that are used in legislation without employing specific legislation itself. We see the attempt made to use public money to emphasize the importance of this government and to educate the young people of Canada and the newcomers to Canada with the idea of the omnipotence and the omniscience of this government which has been so long in power and which has in large measure swallowed its own propaganda. If it serves no other purpose it was useful to discuss these publications for the purpose of emphasizing that if the government is going to spend the taxpayers' money on publications of this kind then they should set up inter-party committees to supervise every one of these publications. That is the only way there can be any assurance of an objective approach to this problem.


But let us recognize also, and I do hope the public will recognize, that we are not merely fighting for the rights of parliament in our discussion here and in such debates as that which just concluded a few days ago, but we are fighting in this country now for the survival of democracy itself. I hope those who discuss these things will recognize the insidious propaganda that is being issued by different departments in the name of information but which is designed to impress upon the people the fact that it is only the Liberal party and its representatives in this house who speak for Canada in international affairs. Look through these publications and see whose names appear. It is only those who will convey the impression of the importance of the government. The fact that democracy as we know it depends upon the interplay of forces between the parties in this House of Commons is completely ignored in the documents that are put before our young people and the members of our forces as a basis for discussions of this kind. I hope this discussion will lead to a reappraisal of the matter by the government. After all, if there has been one encouraging thing in the whole session it has been the recognition that discussion can produce some results, and I would hope that the brief discussion of the publications to which I have referred might mark a change in this respect as well.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I do not wish to prolong the discussion. I have listened with great interest to the speeches on this particular phase of our activities, but I must say that so far as these publications are concerned we do make a serious attempt to make them objective and they are not put out with any idea of propaganda or promotion of any person or party. It is a difficult job to get the right subjects and treat them so the average citizen agrees that the publications are useful.
I want to make it clear that my only interest in these publications as minister is because it has been brought home to me so often that they serve the very useful purposes of adult education, and of keeping our people informed at home and abroad.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I only want to add that I am entirely in favour of providing the members of our armed forces overseas with objective information, but I want to make it clear that what I have seen overseas as well as here does not indicate that it is objective information but on the contrary is heavily loaded information, and I leave for the minister's consideration the possibility of inter-party committees to supervise publications of this kind.

238. War museum, $25,050.

Mr. Chairman, I have been waiting for four years to speak for three minutes on this particular item having to do with the national war museum. It is a subject which, coming at the tail end of the defence estimates, receives no attention and yet deserves some comment. The national war museum is perhaps the smallest government building in the Dominion of Canada. It is very well looked after by those who are in charge and the exhibits are carefully arranged, but hampered by space justice cannot be done to the exhibits available in the hands of those who are in charge of the museum. The exhibits are chiefly representative of world war I and very few exhibits having to do with world war II can be shown because of the limitation of space.
I doubt if there is much in that war museum to indicate other activities of Canadian servicemen in the South African war, the 1885 rebellion, the Fenian raids, the war of 1812 to 1814 and the resistance that was offered by Canadians in 1775 and 1776. I think it is a bit unfortunate that a museum of this nature has not received more attention on the part of the government. I understand it is visited by thousands of people each year. One of the attendants estimates that
100,000	people pass through the museum in the course of a year. It is advertised as one of the tourist attractions of the capital city.
I am going to be very brief, but I should like to draw attention to the comments made by the royal commission on arts, letters and sciences in 1951. At page 323 of the Massey report there is the following under the heading "A Canadian Historical Museum":
We are impressed by the fact that Canada lacks two institutions which are generally considered essential to a civilized people, a national library and a national historical museum. . . . On the necessity for an historical museum we can hardly speak too strongly.
Further on there is this observation:
We observed also that in the public archives is now preserved a valuable collection of historical exhibits other than manuscripts, that the national gallery has in its possession a great number of paintings illustrating Canada's part in the two world wars, and that the Canadian war museum has, with very meagre resources, collected and preserved an important collection of war exhibits. We are also informed that various departments and agencies of government have in their keeping considerable quantities of historical material; all this we consider should now be gathered together, appropriately classified, and suitably exhibited.
On page 324 the royal commission recommended:
That when a suitable building is provided for the historical museum it take over the collections of the present Canadian war museum . . .
50433-387i
Supply-National Defence
I should like to say that I agree with the suggestion of the commission that an historical museum is much better than the maintenance of a museum called a war museum, which title is not very attractive to a non-military people like ourselves. A war museum rather indicates certain things that are distasteful to the minds of people. We do not like to think about war. Gathered together in an historical museum, war exhibits would find their proper place. They are not superior in interest to other matters that have affected the development of a country and nation such as Canada. Nevertheless they should not be neglected, and I think they would find their proper place ini an historical museum.
I should like to suggest to the minister, burdened as he is with many other things of greater importance than a museum collection, that in conference with his colleagues he press for the establishment of an historical museum as recommended by the Massey commission and that he be relieved of the responsibility of the present war museum. As it stands at the moment, to be called a national war museum does not do full justice to the great history of the Canadian people, and I think a rather poor impression is created because of the small size of the building and the small number of exhibits on display. I draw this to the attention of the committee, and urge the minister to take appropriate steps to have some change made. It is a matter of extending it, perhaps over a series of years. But let us look forward to the future and around the time of the 100th anniversary of confederation perhaps we may have established in this country an historical museum which will give due credit to the exhibits that are attributed to our war experiences.
