speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, my staff has prepared a very comprehensive review of world events, and if the temperature were 10 degrees lower I would be inclined to read it. However, I do not think that is really necessary in these trying conditions.
I can report however that the Canadian economy is booming as never before. Our exports are at record levels; capital investment will undoubtedly reach the highest figure on record, and production is also at a very high level. Production is always dependent somewhat upon crop conditions; but the western crop promises to be of almost record proportions, in spite of the slightly lower acreage that was planted this year. I cannot help thinking of my arrival back from Australia and New Zealand, when I was met by newspaper reporters at the airport who insisted upon a television interview. One of the questions asked was as to whether I knew that the prairies were flooded, and that we would have no crop this year. I said, "No, I did not know that"-and I said, furthermore, that I did not believe it. I said, "We never kill western crops on the sixth day of May." They said, "Well, if it is flooded,


you cannot plant it." I said, "It is flooded, but it dries up again, and the wheat is planted and the crop matures." I had more letters about that interview-most of them critical-[DOT] than perhaps regarding any remark I ever made. But perhaps by this time I can say, "The old man was right on that occasion, anyway."
The pick-up in exports started last November. For the first five months of this year the exports are a little over 10 per cent higher than for the previous year. The record of the first five months represents a new record total, and the level of exports as compared with the previous year is rising month by month.
About half the improvement in our exports this year is due to the marked increase in our exports to the United Kingdom. It has been stated in this house many times that we have been losing our markets in England. That has never been true. After the war Great Britain was short of dollars, and is still short of dollars-but not as short as she was previously-therefore her imports from dollar countries had to be sharply curtailed. While for a time the dollar value of our exports slipped somewhat under the value of exports in pre-war years, our proportion of the market did not fall below our proportion in those years. It has always been somewhat higher than our proportion during the pre-war years.
During the first five months of this year the increase has amounted to 37 per cent, which is the sharpest increase we have had in exports to that market. And I am happy to say that our improved position is continuing now that there can be further relaxation of dollar controls. We believe the British market will continue to expand, and that our proportion of the market will continue to grow.
As a matter of fact, of the expansion in imports in the British market during the past five months, half of the increase represents imports from Canada. That is a very satisfactory position. We have also had a substantial improvement in our exports to other commonwealth countries.
I had the privilege of visiting Australia and New Zealand this spring, and while there I discussed credit restrictions with the authorities in both those countries. While there certain relaxations were obtained and are bearing fruit. Our exports to Australia, New Zealand, South Africa and other commonwealth countries are contributing to the substantial increase in exports we are experiencing at the present time.
The United States market slipped off during 1954, owing to the recession in that country. But, as hon. members know, the situation there has been corrected, and our exports

are back to slightly above the levels of 1953 -which was the banner year for exports to the United States.
Therefore I would say the over-all picture is good. There have been some disappointments in countries that we call other than British countries; I am thinking chiefly of South American countries. Their exchange situation has worsened, and there has been no improvement in our exports to "other countries". But with our substantial improvement in exports to British countries, and with an improvement over the record year of exports to the United States, we feel that the situation in that regard is in a very healthy condition indeed.
We have had some disappointments in exports of wheat. Just when a good movement seemed to be getting under way, it has been upset by dock strikes and railway strikes in England, or difficulties in other markets. Nevertheless our exports of wheat and wheat flour are slightly above those of last year, and our sales as of July 1 are substantially above our sales as of July 1 a year ago. So that there is some encouragement in the export situation for wheat and other grains.
Our trading relations with countries of the world are good. I believe our trade commissioner service is doing excellent work. Not only do they report substantial business opportunities, but reports to the department about their work from businessmen travelling abroad are such as to make me feel happy about that service. Our bureau of statistics is maintaining its place as one of the most reliable in the world, and I think our economic branch is doing excellent work in forecasting. I know that the forecasts put out by the Department of Trade and Commerce are highly regarded by those in business interested in the same work, and I believe it is a very efficient branch of the department. Crown companies, for which the department is responsible, seem to be prospering. Atomic energy is still in the expansion stage; it has not actually reached operating level. Eldorado is doing very well indeed. Generally speaking, the business affairs of the department are in a healthy condition.
On this occasion, we are applying for an appropriation of $19,285,000 against $18,789,000 last year, an increase of $496,000 or 2-6 per cent, largely represented by increased salaries to the staff and some increase in the trade commissioners' services. I shall be glad to give more details when we reach the various items where the increase occurs. I may say that more than one-third of the
Supply-Trade and Commerce appropriation is covered by revenue collected by the department. Earnings of grain elevators operated in western Canada by the department and earnings of various services performed for business by the department give a revenue of some $8 million per annum, so that the cost of the Department of Trade and Commerce to the taxpayer is not excessive. I believe the department is rendering full value for the appropriation that is being sought from parliament.

Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, in a recent speech he made in Montreal to the Canadian Manufacturers' Association opened by saying this:
If I were in the House of Commons in Ottawa, I would be confronted with members of the opposition, very friendly people, of course, but just waiting for an opportunity of replying to my speech. I hope, Mr. Chairman, that the rules in this parliament "will allow me the rare privilege of delivering a speech without hearing it torn apart a few minutes later.
I am sure it would be unforgivable to disappoint the minister's expectations in regard to what happens in this house. However, this debate on the first item of the minister's estimates does afford a very precious opportunity of reviewing trade policy, and it is with that thought in mind that I approach the opportunity this afternoon.
Trade is the lifeblood of the Canadian economy. Its importance grows not less but greater all the time. Over 25 per cent of Canadian production goes to the export market. With the possible exceptions of New Zealand and Hong Kong Canada has a greater interest in external trade per capita than any other country.
The minister has made a typical speech, has said the Canadian economy is booming and everything is at a high level. Sir, I think I am inherently an optimist, as much as the minister. Everybody likes to feel optimistic and cheerful; and indeed basically there are extremely sound factors for confidence in the future of Canada. However, sir, in reviewing the estimates of the department and in reviewing matters pertaining to trade policy in Canada, it is our duty today to take an attitude that is searching rather than superficial. I propose to examine a little more deeply some of the factors in the Canadian trade situation and outlook.
The first point that I should like to make, sir, is that growth, constant growth, is imperative in Canada. In the first place, we have a constantly rising population. Last year, Canada's population increased by about 400,000, or approximately 3 per cent. In other words, to hold our own in relation to population, we must be increasing our trade all the time.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
The other factor is this. World trade is growing. This appears in a digest of a recent publication by the United Nations. It is dated June 26:
The world economic picture looks increasingly bright. International trade in the last year marked up a 7 per cent increase over the 1953 record high. Countries long bothered by dollar shortages made some gains. Prices of raw materials stayed stable- with few exceptions-or improved.
Sir, it is against that background that I ask the house to examine the trade position of this country at the present time. Let us bear in mind, then, where we see evidences of growth of Canada's trade, that growth parallels world trade. Where Canada's trade has not been growing, then Canada's trend of trade to that extent has been running counter to the trend of world trade.
Today we are having the first opportunity to engage in a general debate on trade that we have had in some 13 or 14 months. The minister has concentrated his brief review this afternoon on the most recent months of the period. To see the matter in accurate perspective we must look back over the entire period. We must deal with the year 1954 complete and see how, when we are relating the figures for five months of 1955 to 1954, they measure up in the long-range view. What I have to say now in asking the house to consider certain facts is aimed at having a balanced perspective on the whole situation.
I point out these facts, sir: First, in 1954 our imports and exports declined substantially; second, in 1954 Canada dropped from third place to fourth place among the trading nations of the world, being supplanted in third place by Germany whose recovery has been truly remarkable and is a tribute to the prodigious effort, hard work and efficiency of the German people; third, our imports were the highest per capita in the world; fourth, our trade continued to be concentrated to a dangerous degree with one country, namely, the United States; fifth, while there has been some reversal since the turn of the year, nevertheless the problem remains of maintaining the United Kingdom market for our agricultural surpluses; and sixth, on any fair basis of comparison, the exports of raw materials from this country per capita are proportionately the highest in the world. At a time when unemployment has reached a post-war high the government has been complacent and content about this form of export, particularly to the United States, for manufacturing and processing, much of which is bought back by Canadians later in finished form after United States labour has been expended thereon.


This attitude is reflected in a sentence that fell from the lips of the minister in the speech at Montreal to which I referred earlier when he said:
Imports, too, are up proportionately, which is a healthy sign.
The minister has undoubtedly been concentrating much of his satisfaction on growing imports.
Now, sir, it is fair that one should examine the question of government responsibility in relation to trade. We know that in a free economy the growth of trade depends principally upon the initiative of individuals and their willingness to take risks, but we in this country are accustomed to having the government here claim credit for all that is good in trade and reject blame for occurrences that are unfavourable. I say, sir, that the government has a positive role to fulfil in relation to trade. Governments can greatly assist in promoting trade. There are those aids to which the minister referred this afternoon: firstly, promotion of sales through the trade commissioner service and, second, the gathering and supplying of information to traders.
But in a larger sense the most important field of government responsibility in this regard is in the matter of fiscal policy. This is a subject of high importance in relation to trade. Indeed it used to dominate political debate in this country. I mention three aspects of fiscal policy in relation to trade and government responsibility in that respect.
First of all, there is the obvious matter of taxes. Taxes increase the cost of production. To that extent they lay a burden upon producers, whether producing for export or for the domestic market. Governments, and this one in particular, can help both our exporters and our producers for the home market by trying to lower the cost of production, and they can assist very much in that respect by lowering taxes. In that regard also, while this government is calling upon producers where possible to lower their cost of production, we say that the government can set a very good example to producers in that respect by putting its own house in order.
This matter of keeping costs down is a very important one. Indeed the minister, when he returned from Geneva on December 30, said on arriving at Ottawa:
"Prices are coming down all over the world and our price structure will keep pace". Canadian industry would have to keep up with competitive world prices if it wanted to continue in the world trading picture.
I need say no more on that subject.
The second aspect of fiscal policy and government responsibility concerns keeping clear

the export channels for sale of our goods abroad. From time to time we hear discussion in this house about tariffs. Tariffs have greatly receded in significance in the world of today; as compared with other forms of restriction they do not command anything like the importance of other years. They have been supplanted by such restrictive factors as quotas, quantitative restrictions, arbitrary exchange valuations, inconvertibility of currencies, discriminations, customs procedures and other uncertainties. If one were to attempt to define the duty of government in relation to these modern and much more effective forms of restriction, one would say, particularly as applied to our trade relations with the nations that are signatories to GATT, that the duty of the government is to be alert to detect, swift to protest, persuasive and resourceful in seeking removal of these restrictions.
The third aspect of fiscal policy and government responsibility is to ensure fair opportunity to our domestic producers in the domestic market.
There is one general aspect of trade which looms large in the world in which we live.
Supply-Trade and Commerce It is the relationship of trade to peace. So far as Her Majesty's loyal opposition is concerned, we by no means underrate the contribution which world trade has to make to the establishment and maintenance of peaceful relations among nations. Undoubtedly, the more closely nations are knitted together by commercial ties, the more likely they are to seek to preserve their prosperity and stable relations in friendly association. There is one exception in this respect and that is the matter of state trading, which has dangers both political and economic that are only too apparent when attempts are made to cut off sources of supply.

Here may I ask, to save time, that these tables which are in the report might be printed in Hansard by consent? Our exports to the United Kingdom fell successively in 1952, 1953 and 1954. This recovery in 1955 must be measured against that kind of background. The decline in 1954, we are told, "reflected chiefly lower grain requirements". It might be more accurate to say lower grain purchases. But the value of the United Kingdom market is very great for Canada and much yet remains to be done by this government to possess that market.
"Where Britain buys its foodstuffs" is the interesting heading of an article by the Canadian commercial secretary at London, Mr. Bruce Marshall, and appearing in the July 9 issue of the department's publication Foreign Trade. That summary statement will repay some study. The article takes seven foodstuffs for which Britain is dependent in whole or in part upon imports from abroad. Here are the statements. First, there is "flour: Imports totalled 360-8 thousand tons in 1954; nearly 90 per cent came from Canada". We will all agree that that is a very satisfactory report. Second, "wheat: Purchases reached 47 * 4 million bushels in the first quarter of 1955. Canada supplied 20 million bushels". According to my arithmetic, Canada's proportion was 42 per cent in that period and I think all of us would say that it ought to be higher. Third, "butter: Of total imports of 632-5 million pounds in 1954, New Zealand and Denmark together supplied about 90 per cent". Canada supplied not one pound of butter. Fourth, "cheese: About 250 million pounds purchased abroad in 1954; Canada, Australia, New Zealand and South Africa competed for this trade". Note the arrangement of the names of the countries; Canada is the first of the four. It almost suggests to the avid reader that Canada led, but what are the facts?

Taking account of the fact that Canada sold no butter, it would be interesting to know whether, if the government were prepared to offer to the United Kingdom the same favourable terms for butter purchases as those that were recently offered to the government of Czechoslovakia, we might be able to sell some of this surplus butter we have in the United Kingdom market, if it were subsidized to the extent to which the butter sale to Czechoslovakia was subsidized. Then one would like to know why similar terms could not be offered to the United Kingdom on sales made there.
Let me say this, Mr. Chairman. The policies of the United Kingdom favour more trade. Britain is making steady approaches toward convertibility. She has extended the existing quotas, and other restrictions have been removed or reduced. Now is the time to move into that market and to seek to recover it for all these surpluses of agricultural products for which formerly we found a ready and steady market in the United Kingdom. We need to recover more of the United Kingdom market; and when I say "recover" I use that word advisedly, because these markets over the years have been largely lost. This government has always been, in our view, cool and indifferent toward the United Kingdom market. We propose to continue to press for the recognition of the importance of that market and of trading in it.
As to our trade with the United States, I have already pointed out the dangerous extent to which we have been placing our trading eggs in that one basket. By way of rectifying that danger we are of the opinion that efforts should be made to try to sell in other countries and, in so far as we can enable them to buy from us by purchasing from them, help them in that way to acquire a supply of dollars with which to purchase our exportable products. Undeniably the United States has the great advantage of geography and the American producer is ready at all times to give to Canadian consumers quality and service accompanied by aggressive salesmanship and with it not a little dumping as well. The size of our trade with the United States bears some contemplation. It is the largest trade carried on between any two countries in the world. It gives rise to a gigantic trade deficit for Canada. Indeed, it is so large that it could not be sustained were it not for the fact that United States capital has been coming into

Supply-Trade and Commerce this country for investment. Twelve per cent of our national produce is exported to the United States. Only 1 per cent of theirs is exported to Canada.
As best I can I now wish to size up what appear to be some of the dangers that should enter into our policy considerations in reference to United States trade as well as some of the factors that may give us reason for settled confidence. Of these dangers I mention three in particular which are continuing dangers. The first is the attitude of the United States congress and blocs there, particularly the agricultural bloc, which have made their influence felt more than once without regard to the obligations assumed by the United States under GATT. In 1952 it took the form of restrictions on dairy imports from Canada; in 1953, more restrictions on dairy imports; in 1954, quotas on imports of Canadian oats, barley and rye; and in 1955, steps to curtail imports of crude oil from Canada, and hardboard, and the issue there is still in the balance. What is threatened there now is a breach of GATT, and Canada, along with Sweden and Finland, has a direct interest. There were threats in the United States to impose a tariff against the importation of lead and zinc. In 1954 Canada shipped $80 million worth of lead and zinc into the United States market. This matter is one of first importance for Canadian trade. The imposition of a tariff on lead and zinc was only avoided when President Eisenhower decided instead to proceed to stockpile these metals until the end of 1956. The copper duty, which is a matter of very great concern to Canada, has been suspended for another three years ending June 30, 1958, only due to executive action. It looked for a time this year as though a United States tariff was to be directed against the importation of uncooked fish sticks from Canada, a trade that was worth $12 million to Canada last year.
The fact that blocs in congress, particularly the agricultural bloc, did not succeed in erecting further barriers against the importation of Canadian agricultural products is due largely to President Eisenhower. But the attitude that has been revealed in congress is one that has been taken there notwithstanding the provisions of GATT and also notwithstanding the friendly relations that exist between Canada and the United States.
The second danger facing us from that quarter is the sale of United States farm surpluses abroad. Under the agricultural trade development and assistance act passed by congress in 1954 surplus commodities valued at $700 million may be sold abroad over a period of 36 months and in addition

commodities valued at up to $300 million may be given away to friendly peoples abroad in the event of national disaster or famine. It is recognized by the United States administration that the magnitude of United States holdings of many commodities is capable of demoralizing world markets should a policy of reckless selling abroad be pursued.
These huge surpluses and the selling policy at Washington remain a constant threat to Canadian markets abroad, the prices for our agricultural surpluses in those markets, and consequently to the prices of agricultural products here at home. For example, subsidized United States exports of cheese to Belgium adversely affected shipments of Canadian cheddar cheese in 1954. Again, on May 31 the United States and Japan signed an agreement by which Japan will purchase $85 million worth of surplus United States agricultural products and will receive another $15 million worth of such products free, and they include wheat. Considering the way in which Canada is trying to build up its export market for wheat in Japan as well as for other agricultural products that are included in the scope of the agreement between the United States and Japan, we cannot underestimate the gravity for Canada of agreements of this kind based on the selling policy at Washington.
The third continuing danger relates to the United States form of customs administration. This has been for years something of a labyrinth, creating all manner of delays and uncertainties which have greatly impeded the efforts of Canadian exporters to find a way for their goods into the United States market.
I said I was going to say a word about the hopeful features of our trading relations with the United States. There are three that come to mind. The first is the recent enactment by congress of the trade agreement extension act of 1955. It continues for three years the president's authority to cut tariffs without the prior approval of congress in return for trade concessions from other nations, and it also permits the president to make a reduction of 5 per cent in each of the next three years on most items.
But, sir, while we have a sense of relief in the enactment of that measure by congress we have to recall at the same time that it was a compromise, because congress tacked on two additional riders to the bill. The first protects the textile and chemical industries by prohibiting cuts in duties on Japanese goods more than 50 per cent below 1954 levels, and the second gives the president new powers to impose quotas on imports that threaten domestic industries vital to national security.

The second feature is the legislation before congress designed to simplify the customs administration. The fact that there is still hope for this legislation gives us at least a breathing space.
The third, and not least of all, factor of hope in this situation is the attitude of President Eisenhower. He has taken a far-sighted view of the responsibilities of his country to give the world leadership not simply in relation to resistance to aggression and the maintenance of peace by force of arms but also the building of peaceful relations by extending trade relations.
But having regard to the uncertainties of the United States situation and the fact that the administration cannot control congress, Canadians must continue to be vigilant and wary in their dealings with the United States in matters of trade.
As to our trade with other countries, may I say a brief word with regard to the subject of trade with iron curtain countries in the view that the Progressive Conservative party takes with respect to policy in this matter. We are all conscious in recent days of the appearance of a softening attitude on the part of the Kremlin and other countries behind the iron curtain. I suppose all of us approach this with some degree of wariness and caution.
We will remember in the first place that there is still a long list of strategic materials, dating back to the hostilities in Korea, which the countries of the western world have bound themselves not to ship or permit to be shipped to countries behind the iron curtain or through channels by which they may reach countries behind the curtain. In July a year ago the number of commodities on the list of strategic materials was substantially reduced. No doubt this matter is the subject of continuing negotiations, and I hope the minister will make a report to the house as to how these negotiations are faring.
But in the matter of food we in Canada are conscious of our large surpluses for which we are anxious to find a market. We of Her Majesty's loyal opposition see no reason not to sell these surpluses to iron curtain countries just because they happen to be iron curtain countries. In our view it is a question of making a good business deal. In that respect our thinking, it seems to me, is in line with the thinking of the administration at Washington where Mr. Ezra Taft Benson, secretary of agriculture, in a press interview which he gave on December 15 had the following things to say on this subject. He was referring to the fact that the administration at Washington was then considering direct trade in some 50433-3884
Supply-Trade and Commerce farm commodities with iron curtain countries, and he had the following to say:
"My feeling is that we should be willing to trade with iron curtain countries so long as the trade is in our favour, whether it be butter or anything else", Benson told a press conference. He had told the conference "we are considering some sales to countries which may in turn sell to iron curtain countries".
Asked if direct sales to iron curtain countries or to countries which might sell to Russia and its satellites was contemplated, Benson replied "both". Benson made these comments in answer to a question about possible plans to sell butter to Russia.
In January a broker offered to buy surplus United States butter for export to Russia, but the commerce department turned thumbs down on the deal.
As to countries outside the Russian orbit reselling United States goods to iron curtain countries, Benson said it was difficult to police sales to other countries as far as the ultimate destination of the goods was concerned.
Now, sir, with regard to deals such as the two that have been mentioned in recent days, the wheat sale to Poland and the butter sale to Czechoslovakia, we have no objection to the sale of Canadian exportable agricultural surpluses to these countries just because they are iron curtain countries. It is a question in every case of whether it is a good deal for Canada. In both cases, one asks if we could not be equally successful in selling to our friends if we offered them the same favourable kind of terms. In the case of the wheat deal the terms were only 15 per cent cash and 85 per cent credit, while in the case of the deal for butter with Czechoslovakia there was a subsidy which would permit the price to be reduced by 21 cents per pound.

As a matter of fact he has not made any particular comment about it since the announcement of the signing of the agreement last March. So far as we of Her Majesty's loyal opposition are concerned, let me re-emphasize that we have always supported GATT. Right from the time of the signing of the first agreement in 1947 we have supported it. We are not unmindful of the fact that 80 per cent of the trade of the entire world has been carried on under GATT since its inception, and that the binding of tariff items for three years at a time has been of great benefit to exporters in


their forward pricing. And we are not overlooking the extent to which the GATT policy has found its way into the Canadian tariff.
As to the 1955 agreement for renewal, we as a party have withheld comment, chiefly because we have been waiting to see what was going to happen in Washington. We await ratification by the United States congress of the agreement to establish the organization for trade co-operation, which was signed in March. But this review of trade policy could not properly be completed without making one or two comments about GATT.
The 1955 GATT is indeed disappointing. It is disappointing to Canada principally because of two factors. The first of these is that the new agreement definitely favours the United States. That country obtained a waiver in favour of its desired right to impose import restrictions on agricultural imports and to levy fees upon imported agricultural products. In the second place this agreement is disappointing because attempts to eliminate quantitative restrictions, imposed under conditions of balance of payments difficulties, failed. Both these matters are very serious for Canada.

The result is not as good as it might have been, but it might have been much worse.
Sir, as one who has listened to the Minister of Trade and Commerce in this chamber over the last ten years I say that never in that time has the minister, in any comment he has made about anything with which he has been associated, damned it with such faint praise.
Let me sum up our approach to the matter of the 1955 GATT in these words. We must weigh the new GATT agreement in the light of the experience that follows under it. Particularly we must see what use the United States makes of its numerous escape clauses. If the hoped-for benefits under the agreement are destroyed by action on the part of the United States, Canada will certainly find it necessary to regain her freedom of action. The United States should be clearly warned of that fact now. On the other hand, we hope the new agreement may not, by that type of action on the part of the United States, be deprived of its potentialities for good. Vigilance is the duty we lay upon ourselves in this situation.

By reason of time, sir, I come to these final remarks. I have tried to set out the problems and what ought to be, it seems to me, our objectives in trade policy in perspective. We Conservatives regard ourselves as realists. We live in a world of increasing competition. It is also a world of increasing need for the benefits of peace. We must meet the challenge that is offered to us in this increasingly competitive world by increasing our productivity, our efficiency, our service and our salesmanship, and that applies to the government as much as it does to individuals.
We can best do this, all of us, of course, by encouraging initiative and enterprise on the part of Canadian producers. On the part of the government, we look to it to be more vigilant, realistic and successful in the discharge of its duties in relation to trade which I have endeavoured to describe this afternoon as falling within the proper role of government responsibility.
We Conservatives have abundant, unwavering and deep-seated confidence in Canada and the future of Canadians. Using our native intelligence and vigour and resources, applying all the wisdom in research that we can command, with the utmost encouragement to research on the part of the government and using the opportunities that are open to us of increasing the extent to which we fabricate and process these abundant materials with which a beneficent Providence has endowed us, in our view there need be no limit to Canada's future development and growth. We, being realists, think we are entitled to regard ourselves as the true optimists in Canada.
Agreed.

I am not tempted this afternoon with the small attendance in the house, some having returned to their constituencies, to dwell at any length on the trade policies either of the government or of the movement for which I have the honour to speak in this house.
I also want to say this. I was very happy to give the hon. gentleman permission to continue beyond the 40 minutes. But I think in preparing a speech to be delivered in the house in future, having agreed to the new 30-minute rule in committee, we should try to contain our remarks within the 30 minutes. I also very strongly hold to the idea that if one has prepared a speech carefully one can
6136	HOUSE OF
Supply-Trade and Commerce say all that one desires to say, except in very exceptional circumstances, in the compass of 30 minutes. I hope in the next session of parliament we shall all endeavour to abide by the new 30-minute rule much better than we have observed the present 40-minute rule this afternoon.
I wish to say first of all that I appreciate the extensive analysis of Canadian trade we have heard from the hon. gentleman. Much of what he placed before the house this afternoon was worth while. Of course we are living in a very different atmosphere from that in which we lived a few years ago, during the war and in the immediate postwar period. At that time two of the great industrial competitors were out of the world market. There was no German production on the world market, nor was there any Japanese production, and the world was short of almost everything Canada could send abroad.
Some of the best cereal-producing areas of the world had been devastated, and we were called upon to export vast quantities, not only of cereals but of animal products to make up for those normally produced from cereals grown elsewhere in the world. So it was very interesting when the hon. member mentioned in his speech that the British were receiving certain goods from Poland. Well, I read a few days ago that Poland is one of the principal suppliers of bacon and hams to the United Kingdom. On the other hand, of course, Poland takes certain manufactured articles from the United Kingdom.
In this connection, we have to bear in mind that trade has become much more competitive than it was a few years ago. If we are to increase our exports of the products we desire to export, then we must be prepared to accept from customer countries more of the goods they wish to send to us in payment for the goods we wish to send abroad.
I hear a great deal about convertibility. Well, I would like to see convertibility among the currencies of the world, and particularly as between sterling and the dollar. But to my mind it is quite unrealistic to talk about convertibility unless you realize that convertibility must be based upon an exchange of goods. Unless you are prepared to exchange goods with the sterling areas, I cannot see how you are going to convert sterling into dollars or dollars into sterling. After all, in the final analysis trade is an exchange of goods and services.
It seems to me that when we talk about certain industries and ask the Minister of

Mr. Chairman, I agree with the hon. member for Eglinton that much needs to be done to rehabilitate the British market, and I also agree with the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar that a great deal of the responsibility for bringing about convertibility of currencies will have to rest with the dollar area. It is true that we have been repeatedly told for some years that progress is being made toward convertibility, but it is interesting to note that 45 of the 56 member nations of the international monetary fund are still imposing restrictions on monetary transactions under article 14 of that fund. Although the five-year limit on these restrictions expired in 1952, these nations are still unable to accept the obligations imposed upon them under article 8.
I would say that any attempt today to bring about convertibility would lead to excessive import restrictions in order to protect the balance of payments of those sterling nations, and if that were done the result, of course, would be that we would have greater surpluses piling up within the dollar area.
One of the major problems we have had to face in recent years has been this question of getting surplus goods to needy nations. A good deal was said about that matter yesterday. I have spoken on this question. But we were speaking to the Minister of Agriculture, and in my opinion he is not the minister who can deal with the problem. That problem can only be dealt with by the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Finance, and of the two I would


say that probably the greater responsibility will have to rest with the Minister of Finance.
But we have this very unhappy situation. According to Mr. Hambidge, who spoke before the Senate on May 11 and who is the North American regional representative of the food and agriculture organization, 50 per cent of the people of the world are on the verge of starvation, hungry and dying young. But they know it is possible for them to have a far better standard of living. He points out that this knowledge is causing a great deal of international friction and is making it possible for people who are trying to stir up trouble to capitalize on that situation.
If it were not possible to supply goods to these people there would not be the same amount of discontent. But when these people know it is possible, and see in the western world steps being taken to reduce production while they are starving, naturally it creates a good deal of international friction. In the United States, of course, a certain price for wheat has been guaranteed contingent upon a reduction of acreage. That is not so in Canada.
On the other hand there is no doubt that the present situation is having a tendency to discourage production, or to discourage an increase in agricultural production. The Canadian Federation of Agriculture even went so far as to say that a support price should not be an incentive price. In other words they are afraid that if prices are too high the farmers will increase their production and cause surpluses. The Minister of Agriculture made a similar statement about increased production. He said farmers might get less for increased production than they got for the lesser production.
When that statement is made by the Minister of Agriculture and by farm organizations, naturally you are discouraging any increase in the production of agricultural goods and, as I say, when you have a situation where half the peoples of the world are hungry and dying young through lack of food, it is a highly undesirable situation.
Yesterday I quoted a statement made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I am going to refer to that statement again, because I have an idea the Minister of Trade and Commerce might agree with it. It is a statement he made during the election campaign, when he spoke at Viking. It was published in the Edmonton Journal. He stated:
I've heard Social Crediters say we should reduce our stocks of wheat by accepting foreign currencies or even by giving them away.
This has an appeal when we see our wheat piling up whilst others starve, but in Ottawa we have an obligation to keep trade on solid ground. If we

started bartering or giving away, we would disturb international markets and in the long-run we would injure not only ourselves but also those we seek to help.
We should try to keep trade on a multilateral, economic basis and disregard emotional superficial solutions to our problems.
I do not know whether the Minister of Trade and Commerce would suggest that the acceptance of foreign currency or barter deals would be a superficial emotional policy. I find it hard to believe that the Secretary of State for External Affairs really believes that, because after all he is working in close association with the United Nations Organization, and one of the main proposals put forward to date by the food and agriculture organization has been the international commodity clearing house. Under that proposal the FAO advocated the sale of goods for foreign currencies. Hence, as I say, I find it hard to believe that the Secretary of State for External Affairs would feel that the acceptance of foreign currency would really be a superficial solution.
I want to say a few words on the international commodity clearing house, because the FAO council set up a body of six experts to make a detailed study of the whole problem of getting rid of surpluses. This is the recommendation they brought down.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
May I ask my
hon. friend a question?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Have I succeeded yet in pointing out to him that whether it is a pound note or a dollar note, it does not constitute foreign currency? Also does he say that if we accepted payment in pounds and we spent pounds in Europe, we solved everything? Is that his view? By accepting foreign currency we interpret the meaning as being unexpendable currency.
I shall deal with that matter very shortly, because I do not agree with the minister at all and I think I can prove he is wrong. He gave us a story the other day-

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: You will have to speak a long time if you wish to change my mind. I am stating facts.
I am stating facts too. Somebody told you that story in England and he was just pulling your leg, or you were just pulling our leg.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I can quote an official statement.

That was not an official statement, the one you gave us. You told us a story that some man told you in England. As
Supply-Trade and Commerce I say, that man was having a great laugh or pulling your leg, because it could not possibly be based on fact.
It was a good story, anyway.
It was not even a good story.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Let us have your theory; then we will submit your theory to the Bank of England.

No, I do not think it is necessary. I shall be able to deal with that point quite fully when I come to it. It is interesting to note how the minister tries to divert me from the recommendations of the FAO, to which I wanted to refer. After all, that committee set up by the FAO made a detailed study of this whole situation. These are the recommendations they brought in. The minister should talk to them if he wants to convert them to his idea. The recommendations they made were as follows:
(1)	Subject to provisions outlined below, the purchase of stocks of commodities that are in surplus in the country in which those stocks appear.
(2)	The negotiation of sales in inconvertible currencies in order to assist in maintaining the flow of trade during periods of exchange disequilibrium; such payments being guaranteed by the buying countries against losses from exchange depreciation.
(3)	The negotiation of sales at special prices below the market to countries in need, under strictly defined conditions of use: for example, for relief purposes, special nutritional programs, or for development projects.
(4)	As a long run function, the holding of stocks acquired in periods of surplus as reserves to protect the interests of consumers in periods of shortage.
(5)	The negotiation of bilateral or multilateral trading agreements, or exchanges of commodities on a barter basis.
Then it goes on to explain how we could have sold under that provision and it states:
(1) The exporting country would sell surplus wheat to the international commodity clearing house at full market price and the purchases would be financed by the exporter contributing the value of the wheat to international commodity clearing house as additional capital. International commodity clearing house would then sell quantities of wheat to the importing country in addition to and not as a substitute for its usual purchases. ICCH would take in payment the currency of the importing country, even if it were, at the time, inconvertible.
As I say, that is the statement by a body of experts who have given this matter a detailed study. They evidently do not agree in any way with the suggestions made by the minister in this regard.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs suggested that we should be satisfied to resume normal channels of trade on sound policies. What are those sound policies? In

Supply-Trade and Commerce 1945 the government supported the Bretton Woods agreement. We spent a great deal of time in this house discussing it. The Bretton Woods agreement was based very largely upon the White plan, the plan of a man who has since been denounced by the F.B.I. as a communist.
It is very interesting to note that when the Bretton Woods agreement was first brought up its strongest supporters were the communists in this country, the labour progressive party. They denounced everybody in the country as a fascist who opposed the Bretton Woods agreement. But the interesting point to note is that none of the communist countries became members of the Bretton Woods agreement. They did everything they could to push the capitalistic nations into it; and having got the capitalistic nations into it they very wisely, I think, kept out of it themselves.
We opposed the Bretton Woods agreement on the ground that it did not follow the fundamental principle of international trade which is, we claim, the exchange of goods and services among nations on a basis of mutual advantage. If nations are going to exchange goods, then surely the only currency they need is the currency of the importer because it is that currency that will buy the importer's goods. At the time we were discussing the Bretton Woods agreement we were repeatedly told that the situation would be improved and the difficulties of the nations would be largely overcome if an international trade organization were formed. But unfortunately when that organization was formed the problem was still further aggravated by a policy of nondiscrimination, which denied a nation the right to place restrictions against imports from a country with which it had an unfavourable balance of trade, except through escape clauses.
I think we must agree that any agreement which has to depend almost entirely upon escape clauses in order to function is not a very strong agreement. The international trade organization agreement-that is the Geneva trade agreement today-has been more honoured in the breach than in the observance, and the same thing can be said of the Bretton Woods agreement. As a matter of fact, international trade would have collapsed many years ago, it would have collapsed during the war, if it had not been for the fact that the United States introduced lend-lease. Under lend-lease it will be remembered that the United States exported goods to Europe and accepted payment in kind. It ended in an understanding that they would accept payment in kind, that is, that

they would accept payment in goods. For the time being the dollar sign was largely abolished.
Later on the Marshall plan was introduced. Under the Marshall plan the United States made dollars available to Europe to buy United States goods, and Canada benefited very greatly under that proposal because many of the dollars that European nations obtained from the United States were spent in Canada. More recently a program has bpen adopted under the agricultural adjustment act by which the United States is making goods available to European nations and other nations of the world in exchange for their currency. Last year somewhere in the neighbourhood of $1,400 million worth of goods were disposed of under that program.
It is quite obvious that since 1945 we have not been operating under the Bretton Woods agreement or under the Geneva trade agreement. We have only been able to operate and maintain trade at a high level as the result of a number of programs put into operation by the United States, which were put into operation largely to make it possible for European and other nations to buy United States goods.
Last year the minister suggested on several occasions that the United States program would not get very far. He actually told members of the house that he did not know of any nation that would be willing to buy goods from us in exchange for their own currency, but in spite of that the United States has greatly expanded its program and today is selling many goods for the currency of the importing nation.
I was rather interested in a press dispatch from London found in the Ottawa Journal of Tuesday, June 28, headed "Selling Policies Put U.S. in Front of Wheat Exporters". The dispatch reads in part as follows:
The Financial Times says Canada has lost her leadership among wheat exporting nations because the United States has a "more progressive selling policy". The United States is "prepared to export wheat tor local foreign currencies-which Canada has not yet been prepared to do". Accordingly, the United States now ranks first as an exporter of wheat, says the newspaper, without elaborating its reference to Canada.
Yet the Minister of Trade and Commerce tried to make us believe last year that foreign nations would not be willing to buy our produce in return for their own currencies. This question was before the house the other day, and when the Minister of Trade and Commerce replied he made a few comments with regard to the acceptance of

foreign currencies. As found at page 3843 of Hansard of May 17, he said:
If we buy goods for sterling, we buy it under a program that has to be worked out with the chancellor, which limits the use of that sterling. Sterling is not freely interchangeable.
I should like to say there that of course agreements have to be reached. All these foreign currencies are under some form of exchange control, and therefore agreements will have to be made under any kind of agreement that is entered into. But what I would be interested in hearing from the minister would be what discussions have taken place to date between the Canadian government and the British government with a view to the acceptance of their currency. As found at page 3844 the minister stated:
When we buy goods in Britain we convert dollars into sterling to pay for those goods. If we had sterling in Britain which we had accepted for wheat which could be used for that purpose, we would be very glad to have that sterling.
I would point out that when we sell goods to Britain we sell for dollars. The minister says we change those dollars into sterling and then buy goods from Britain with that sterling. Why go through the double motion? Rather than sell goods to Britain for dollars, then change the dollars into sterling and spend the sterling in Britain, why not accept sterling in the first place instead of having a double transaction? The advantage to Britain would be very definite, because they would have the assurance that we were going to buy goods from them in return for the goods we had sold them; but when we demand payment in dollars they have no assurance whatsoever that those dollars will be used to buy goods in their country.
Then the minister made this statement, which perhaps I had better read. It is found at page 3846 of Hansard:
Perhaps I might be permitted to relate a small example concerning a friend of mine. This person was visiting in England and had a sort of windfall in the form of sterling. He tried to deposit that sterling in a Canadian bank, but the Canadian bank would not have it at all. Finally he gave it to his lawyer, and his lawyer instructed him that he could use it to pay his personal expenses, such as hotel bills and the like. But he was told that if he bought a necktie or a suit of clothes with it he would be subject to heavy penalty.
I do not know whether the minister's friend was pulling his leg or whether the minister is trying to pull our leg, but that is the most fantastic story I have ever heard. There is not one word of truth in it. I am not suggesting the minister is not telling the truth, but the story itself is not true. I have gone through the same experience myself and I know that a number of other people did the same thing when I told them what I had
Supply-Trade and Commerce done. In 1949 I had an estate left me in England. I went to the Royal Trust Company, told them that I did not know the lawyers handling it in England, and that I wanted the estate handed over to them. I told them I wanted the capital transferred to Canada as soon as possible. It could not be transferred then so it just remained there, and I had the money deposited with a Canadian institution.
The minister said that could not be done, but I deposited it with the Royal Trust Company in England and they held it for me. After waiting a year or so and still not being able to use it, I thought if I could spend some of the money in England maybe I could export the goods to Canada. At that time I needed a new herd bull, a Red Poll. Some of the best herds of Red Polls are in England, so I decided I would try to get an exceptionally good bull there. I wrote to Harry Hobson and asked him to go up to Paul Stuart's farm in Suffolk and pick out for me the best bull he could. I also mentioned what I was doing to the Minister of Agriculture, and he suggested that maybe Mr. Robinson could go up there and inspect the bull. However, Harry Hobson, who is a well known valuator, agreed to take the responsibility of inspecting the bull and deciding whether it was what I wanted.
I also wrote to the Royal Trust Company and asked them to get a permit for the export of the bull. There was no trouble at all. It was just a routine procedure. I paid around $1,200 for the bull and exported it to Canada. Yet the minister says you cannot even buy a necktie. It is fantastic. When I went back home I told two of my neighbours, whom I knew had estates left to them in England, what I had done. They are well known as two of the best stock breeders in that part of the country and they wanted to obtain some outstanding sheep and hogs. They did exactly the same thing. They got Harry Hobson to buy them and they exported the sheep and hogs to this country, using the sterling that had been left to them in England. Now, there would have been justification in that case for Britain refusing us the use of that sterling because it had not earned dollars. But when you ship goods to Britain and take sterling, that sterling has already earned dollars; therefore why would Britain refuse to allow us to use that sterling to purchase goods from Britain? Why would not Britain give us sterling instead of dollars if that sterling has earned dollars?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
We will take all the free spendable sterling Britain wants to give us.

Supply-Trade and Commerce

That is all we have ever suggested. We have suggested we should sell goods for inconvertible sterling, and then spend that sterling in Britain. There is every reason why Britain would prefer to do that instead of giving us dollars. If Britain on the other hand has to pay us in dollars, we will take them and give them to the United States. Last year we sold about $600 million worth to Britain, and Britain sold us about $400 million.
We could have entered into an agreement with Britain to spend the sterling in some other part of the sterling area. We would have to make an agreement on that, of course. We could not make any transaction without it, but there is no trouble as I pointed out. It is just a routine procedure to get that agreement. I suppose the Royal Trust Company telephoned the Bank of England and said, "We want to export so much livestock." They said, "Sure thing, go ahead." There was no difficulty, no trouble. I think, therefore, the minister has either had his leg pulled by somebody or he is magnifying the difficulties. I am satisfied that the acceptance of inconvertible sterling would be quite a help in balancing our trade with the sterling area.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: In that case, Mr. Chairman, I shall make an offer now. I will accept all the freely convertible sterling that Britain wants to give us.
Believe me, that would be a help.

I am not suggesting it be convertible into dollars. If you are talking about convertible sterling that is another thing entirely. Convertible sterling means that it can be converted into dollars, so you may as well take dollars in the first place.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I will put it this way. I will take any sterling that can be spent in England and carry with it the right to an import permit.

If the government will go ahead and make that proposition to England, giving all the assurances that we will not demand dollars from England in place of that sterling, I am satisfied he will be able to make a deal.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I have made an offer.

There are thousands of deals made. I have outlined one and I know of another half dozen farms in the same district that have made deals. If I know of a half a dozen, there must be thousands of deals right across Canada.
Now, the United States is expanding its program for trade on that basis, and at least


it is getting surplus goods to people who need them. I think that is an achievement today. They may not be reducing their surplus by very much because they are producing just as fast as they sell, even under this plan. If they had started this program a few years ago they might not have built up their surpluses to the high levels they have reached at the present time. I believe that instead of deploring what the United States is doing, we should do the same thing.
I was very glad to hear what the minister said. As long as he makes that proposition to the British, without tying too many strings to it, I believe something could be worked out. However, he had better consult the Minister of Finance to see what he has to say about it, because there must have been some strong antagonism to it in the past. I am satisfied one of the main reasons we rejected the proposal of the FAO concerning the international commodity clearing house was because it was objected to by the international monetary fund.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: You will notice the currencies referred to by the FAO are inconvertible currencies.
Yes, that is the kind of currency I am asking you to get from Britain, inconvertible sterling that could only be used to buy goods in Britain.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That is not inconvertible sterling.
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Inconvertible sterling cannot be used to buy anything.

Look at what they say here. They advocate the negotiation of sales in inconvertible currencies. Then they describe how it might work. The international commodity clearing house would take payment in the currency of the importing country, then they buy their goods and put the balance to the credit of the exporter. If you are going to take convertible currency you may just as well take dollars in the first place, because we know what Canada would do just as soon as she got convertible sterling. She would convert it to dollars and pay them to the United States. This has always been the pattern of trade in the past, and that is the policy Mr. Ilsley expounded in this house year after year. He said we have to be able to sell enough goods to Britain to get dollars from Britain to make up our deficit in the United States. I believe I have his actual statement here.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Less so now than ever before.

Well, less so now, perhaps, but that was very definitely the policy in Canada. On April 11, 1946, at page 764 of Hansard, Mr. Ilsley said:
We must be able to use the proceeds of our exports to the United Kingdom and the continent of Europe in paying our own debts in the United States.
At page 919 of Hansard for April 16, 1946, I asked:
Will Canada be prepared to accept goods from the United Kingdom in payment of loans? How will the United Kingdom maintain convertibility of the pound if Canada and the U.S.A. do not provide the United Kingdom with dollars by purchasing British goods to the extent of the British credit?
Then Mr. Ilsley said:
It is not necessary that there should be an adverse balance of payment between Canada and the United Kingdom in order to enable the United Kingdom to repay the loan.
Further down the page Mr. Ilsley said:
She can pay for Canadian goods by export to other countries as well as to Canada, under a multilateral trading system and convertible currencies.
That is fine, but as long as all the dollar countries insist upon maintaining a favourable balance of trade with Britain, how can Britain possibly get the dollars to pay for the goods or pay for her indebtedness in the dollar area. She needs all the dollars she gets to pay for a certain percentage of her imports. She is not able to pay for the balance she wants because we are not balancing our trade with her.
The minister says that is not the case to such a great extent today as it was then. Apparently the Canadian government is still favouring the idea of getting dollars instead of sterling so these dollars can be paid to the United States. But I would say that if convertibility of currency today is nearer than it has been in the past, it is very largely the result of the nations in the sterling area placing restrictions against imports from the dollar area. As I pointed out, 45 of the 56 member nations of the international monetary fund are doing that at the present time.
It must be obvious that to convert, the nation must have access to dollars or to the currency they convert to. It could only be achieved through a balance of trade or by foreign investment. I was interested in what the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar had to say on this question of having to balance our trade with the sterling areas in order to have convertibility. It goes beyond that. The dollar area must buy enough goods from the sterling area to allow it to actually have a favourable balance of trade, since unless it has a favourable balance of trade it cannot maintain a balance of payments because of
Supply-Trade and Commerce the large amounts owed to the dollar areas. Therefore they will have to be able to get more dollars from the dollar areas than they have to pay for their imports if they are ever going to be able to maintain a balance of payments. In my opinion it is useless to talk about the convertibility of currencies unless we-when I say "we" I mean we in the dollar area-are prepared to invest enough in the sterling area to make up the unfavourable balance of payment. It seems to me that the problem of convertibility today is more the obligation or responsibility of the dollar area than the sterling area, because after all how can the sterling area afford to lift restrictions on imports until such time as the dollar area is prepared to balance its trade with the sterling area.
That is something I would like the minister to deal with. I would like him to explain just how the sterling area can hope to lift all their restrictions on imports from the dollar area unless we are prepared to balance our trade with them. Otherwise they are bound to use up their reserves and have an unfavourable balance of trade and an unfavourable balance of payments, unless we are prepared to make capital investments in those countries in the same way the United States is making capital investments in this country, thereby helping us to maintain the balance of payments with the United States.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I always enjoy this debate on trade, because the opposition proves conclusively to me that it is impossible for Canada to have trade. For a long time we traded only because of the Marshall plan, we were told; the United States was sending dollars abroad under the Marshall plan, and we were getting them back with our trade.
Would the minister permit a question. Does he feel that he is now closing the debate? Because I wish to make some comment.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
We are in committee.
We are told there is always some reason why we cannot expect to have trade. We cannot trade with England because our trade is not in balance with England, and we should not trade with the United States because too much of our trade goes to that country. It is almost the only free market in the world, almost the only completely free market, and we think it is a valuable market for us. But opposition members always object to our volume of trade in that market. They say we should not trade with our next door neighbour, the United States.

We do not say that at all.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
Nonsense.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: You always object to our balance of trade with the United States, the proportion of our trade with that country.
It is dangerous.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Then what should we do about it? You say it is dangerous; how can we avoid the danger? That is the silly argument we hear from hon. members opposite each year, that we should not trade with the United States because it is dangerous. However, we are able to maintain our trade on a stable basis and, except for a setback in 1954, the volume of our trade has increased steadily from year to year. And this year will see a new record established for the volume of our export trade.
Hon. members always like to make suggestions about wheat; that we should sell our wheat for almost anything. As a matter of fact we sell wheat for cash. That is the policy of the wheat board, and it is never departed from. Other countries have various ways of financing sales abroad. The United States has its export-import bank, and other countries have various government plans for subsidizing exports and issuing credit.
We have nothing of the kind. We do have the Export Credits Insurance Corporation, which is established as a financially sound agency, its purpose being to help Canadian trade. That insurance corporation does a big business. Last year it insured exports to the value of $36,304,840. That was in the year 1954. Last year we also insured exports to the value of $28,203,887 under section 21 of the act. Since article 21 was included in the act-in 1948-we have insured under this section exports to the extent of $48 million, where the risk has been carried by the federal government. The insurance carried by the federal government covers risks that are too big for the corporation to take on, without reinsurance. The insurance corporation has limited capital. As a matter of prudent operation it must diversify its risks, so that the financial troubles of any one country will not jeopardize the solvency of the insurance company.
On that $48 million the government has insured through the insurance corporation, not one cent has been lost. The total amount excluding insurance still in force has been repaid. In addition the insurance company has turned over to the government about half a million dollars in premium money. Under section 21 the insurance company keeps 25 per cent of the premiums to cover expense of operation, and the balance is

turned over to the government where the government is the co-insurer of the risk.
We had an inquiry through a broker-we call it a trade inquiry-as to whether we should insure a shipment of wheat to Poland. We examined the financial position of Poland and its record in post-war years in the matter of paying its debts. As a business matter, and with the advice of the insurance officials and the financial officials of the government, we replied that we would be agreeable to insuring a risk of about $20 million for low-grade wheat to Poland. As I say, the sale itself was a cash sale. The dealer had to find $20 million to pay the wheat board in order to buy the wheat. But the insurance company, in the ordinary course of business and with the approval of the government, undertook to insure 85 per cent of the sale. This insurance was a separate transaction from the financing.
Now we are told that we gave a great advantage to Poland in doing so. It was no greater advantage than we are prepared to give any country. But if anyone considers it is a great advantage to a person to buy an automobile for 15 per cent down and 85 per cent on credit, as against another person who can pay cash for the car-well, I question whether that statement is accurate. That is exactly the situation with Poland. In addition to the cost of the wheat, which was the same as the cost to anybody else, they had to pay financial charges to the banks, and they had to pay the premium to the insurance company for the insurance coverage.
I do not know why we have to have all this hullabaloo. Ordinarily we do not discuss current sales in this house, and I think we have jeopardized the position of the wheat board in making sales of the same nature. And I might tell you that after the low-grade crop of last year, the sale of $20 million worth of No. 5 wheat is a sale of some value to this country.
Now, I suggest that is all very well to talk politics about wheat transactions, but it does not help the government in the serious problem of the disposal of Canada's wheat crop. I hope we will hear no more about the Polish transaction. The transaction has been completed to the extent of 50,000 tons. I hope Poland will buy the other 200,000 tons; and if they do we are prepared to insure it. But after this airing of the situation in the House of Commons, and the comments made by the Leader of the Opposition, I would not be at all surprised if Poland said, "We will take the 50,000 tons, but you can keep the rest of it." I say that seriously. I hope that critical comments will not be repeated; for the discussions we have on markets for our

wheat simply invite our competitors to move into those markets and see if they cannot take the business from us. I think these remarks are very unfortunate indeed.
Reference has been made to GATT. We were not happy about GATT. We had situations there to which we objected. We spoke strongly against the agricultural exemptions demanded by the United States government and we voted against them. Nevertheless we had to face the fact that the United States were in a position where they were doing what the exemptions legally permitted them to do, for the reason that their domestic laws made it impossible for them to do otherwise.
We sincerely hope these exemptions will not be used to our disadvantage. After the vote had been taken, after the exemptions had been granted, our representatives spoke and said that regardless of the exemptions, we would expect the United States to follow the normal pattern of trade and follow the principle of fair shares. Since then we have seen no deviation from those two principles. They have followed the normal pattern of trade, in spite of the fact that the tariff commission has recommended actions that would deviate from that pattern, nevertheless the principle of fair shares has been followed.
I am confident that they will continue to do so in the interests of peace in the world and good neighbourly relations with Canada.
We are troubled by their policy of selling for foreign currencies, with an undertaking that the currencies will be retained in the importing country. That is very difficult competition indeed to meet. As I said before, it has not been serious in our big markets, but it has been very serious indeed in our smaller markets. Much trade has been lost to the United States for that reason. We are told that a shocking situation has arisen this year, that the United States is exporting more wheat than Canada. Well, they did that in 1951 and 1952. It is not unusual for the United States to export more wheat than Canada, although normally we have been the larger exporting country of the two.
Will the hon. member for Acadia remind me of what he asked me to explain? What was it he wanted me to deal with?
How do you expect the sterling area can remove restrictions against the dollar area unless the dollar area is prepared to balance its trade with the sterling area?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
That is true; nevertheless dollars are earned in various ways. Dollars are earned through direct exchange of goods. They are also earned indirectly through shipping and through insurance. The tourist dollar is also valuable. The
Supply-Trade and Commerce dollar earnings of the colonies make a great contribution. For instance, the West Indies are great earners of dollars through sales of sugar and other commodities to the dollar area. The Far East is also a great earner of dollars through sales of rubber and other commodities, which sell for dollars. Then there are the oil possessions of England abroad. Oil is a dollar earner. The sales of oil as an international commodity are usually made in dollars.
The minister will agree that trade with the dollar area must be such that Britain will get enough dollars to pay for the goods she wants to buy from us.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes; there is no other way.

That is not usually the case. At the recent meeting in Washington between Mr. Howe, Mr. Schneider and the British minister, Canada agreed that Britain should impose restrictions against Canadian goods in order to make it possible for them to build up their dollar reserves.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes. If the restrictions are necessary they must be made, nevertheless my hon. friend will note that during the past two years Britain's reserves of gold and dollars have risen tremendously.
They have been going down.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: They may be going down slightly at the moment, but when he suggests the theory that every country in the world must balance its trade with every other country he suggests an impossible situation.

No; I said the sterling area must actually have a favourable balance of trade with the dollar area because it owes a lot of money to the dollar area. If she is ever going to be able to pay that money she has to have a favourable balance of trade.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That is true; she has to have a balance of trade to allow her to pay current operating expenses plus any debts she owes in those countries. I am happy to say that Britain has got into that position. Just recently there has been a slight drop in their gold and dollar position. They have made a remarkable recovery over the last two or three years.
Was that mainly owing to the strike?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I could not say. Of course the strike contributed to it, because it stopped exports. I daresay they lost orders
6146	HOUSE OF
Supply-Trade and Commerce through their inability to export. These things come and go. We all have setbacks, and Britain has, no doubt.

Will the minister tell me whether deals could be made by which Canada would accept sterling that would be spent in Britain? I would not call that free sterling. Free sterling could be exchanged for dollars. Would Canada be prepared to accept sterling from Britain that could be spent in England or in the sterling area? I am sure they would be glad to exchange them to the extent that we could use them. If we could use sterling where we ordinarily accept dollars we would then be exchanging dollar goods for sterling.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Use sterling to buy abroad?

No. Could we agree to accept sterling from Britain and agree that Canada could use that sterling to buy goods either in Britain or in some other part of the sterling area? If we could enter into such an agreement with Britain, then many of the goods we import from the United States today could be imported from the sterling area, because after all those goods are produced in the sterling area.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: All I can point out to my hon. friend is that there is not the slightest difference between that transaction and a transaction carried out in dollars.
Yes, there is.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Not the slightest. Whether the note is a dollar bill or a pound note, provided they will both buy goods in the country there is no difference between them.
