The only difference is that at times the United States has a very large favourable balance of trade with the rest of the world. Until such time as the United States consistently buys more in proportion to what she sells, it is going to be very difficult to have convertibility of currency, unless of course the United States will invest to make up the difference.
May I ask-

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: My hon. friend is talking about the balance of trade between countries; but as long as countries in Europe are able to obtain from any source the dollars they need to carry on, what difference does it make if it is in balance with that country?
I am talking about the balance between the sterling area and the dollar area.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That is the only way you can balance dollars against sterling. What other way is there of doing it?
I was also thinking of the question of balancing trade between nations.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The hon. member says we must balance trade between Canada and the United Kingdom in order to have our currency convertible. That is not true. But I agree you must balance trade between the dollar area and the sterling area.
We are not far apart.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I am happy to say that for the month of May our trade was almost in balance, and we are very glad indeed to see it come into balance; but we operate a free economy in this country. People can spend their money where they like. I do not know how you can tell people that they should buy in England when they wish to buy in the United States unless you put on currency restrictions, which I am sure every Canadian is anxious to avoid.
I think an educational campaign would help the situation.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
We try to do
that. We have committees here, dollar-sterling committees, and there are others. If my hon. friend will convert the people in his town that will be a contribution. In any event, we have a viable economy here. Statements have been made to the effect that we have a trading deficit with the United States and with the world. That is only a commodity deficit. It does not include gold. I presume we produce around $200 million worth of gold in this country. It does not cover capital transactions, and it does not cover certain indirect earnings which may or may not be balanced in our favour; nevertheless there has been no impairment of our dollar and gold reserves in the last several years in spite of the fact that in three of those years we have had commodity deficits in our balance of trade.
I do not know that there are any other points I need to cover at this time.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few remarks on certain aspects of the discussion which we have had already. First of all, it is pleasant to see the minister back in his old optimistic mood, to which we have become so accustomed and which we like so much.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: He has never been out of it.

There was a little cloud on the horizon last December. I hold in my

hand an editorial from the Winnipeg Free Press of December 29 which was a little troubled about the fact that the minister was not just a ray of sunshine at that time, because they felt that when the minister expressed anything but optimistic views it was almost alarming. Indeed, they say, "His restraint about next year may therefore be read almost like a cry of despair from anyone else."
It is perhaps a good thing for the minister that he had that mood, because now that he is back in an optimistic mood it may be all the more convincing. The Free Press took it upon itself to admonish him to be more optimistic. I am sure he took it in good part. They said in the same editorial of the 29th of December:
Certainly there is no reason to jump the other way and think that, when Mr. Howe for once is cautious, the prophets of recession and doom may for once be right.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I should like to comment briefly on a few of the things that have been said. I was sorry the minister did not speak at greater length in his opening remarks, but he can supplement them as he goes along. We are accustomed to talk about ourselves as an exporting nation, and we know that is true. A figure was given some years ago which was in vogue for some time -I do not know whether the minister will wish to correct this now-to the effect that about three out of eight employed persons in Canada depended directly or indirectly on export trade.
I suppose we can divide our export periods roughly into four: the period when furs were the great export; then the period of wood products, which I suppose persisted during a great part of the nineteenth century right down to nearly the end of the century, when wheat pushed forward and became the great export. Now, I take it, we have base metals and a wide variety of things which have become a very important part of our exports.
We remember the post-war situation here, the boom based on pent-up world demand for consumer goods and also on large capital construction, which indeed still goes on. I suppose the only real anxiety we have in looking at that situation is to observe that as time has gone on our exports have continued to be, perhaps increasingly, from the extractive industries. We have already found that this raises a certain problem, because the extractive industries do not supply proportionately as much employment as the general manufacturing industries.
I want to read into the record two or three remarks I found interesting on that subject
Supply-Trade and Commerce from the London Economist of May 28, in which they raised this question about the extractive industries. It says this on page 745: Can this country continue to lean as heavily as it now does on extractive industries and go on finding employment for its rapidly increasing population?
I digress for a moment to recall that the hon. member for Eglinton earlier in the afternoon drew attention to the serious plight of several of the consumer goods industries. Of course that goes to the very root of the question of employment, because employment more and more depends on the tremendous improvement in the efficiency of machinery, and we And that the extractive industries employ comparatively few people. We spend hundreds of millions on the construction of a project like Kitimat and other great development plants, but once they are in operation a few men with a few levers can run the whole thing.
Would the hon. member speak to us instead of just across the floor?

I continue to read from the Economist:
Reliance on the extractive industries means heavy dependence on foreign markets and suggests a second question: Must Canada remain dependent on exports for its prosperity, or can it gradually grow into a more self-contained economy?
That obviously raises the question of immigration, but we shall hear more about that on another occasion. I want to read something in the same sense from page 746.
Would the hon. member tell us what he is reading from?

I am reading from the London Economist of May 28, at page 746:
An immediate and drastic drop in employment is characteristic of the production stage of a new project. It took hundreds of men to build the iron ore railway into Labrador, or the aluminium smelters at Kitimat; but their continuing operation is so highly mechanized that labour requirements are reduced to a minimum.
The orthodox answer to this dilemma is that the successful operation of new mines and smelters and oil wells spreads prosperity throughout the economy. To some extent this has been demonstrated by Canadian experience in the last eighteen months, when the expansion of the service industries has been the main balance to under-employment in other sectors. But there remains an uneasy feeling that this may not be a complete answer. People want to see some of this prosperity shared by the secondary manufacturing industries, which are better employers of labour than either the mines or the farms.
It is precisely at this point that the present weakness of the Canadian economy is most apparent. General manufacturing, though taking far less capital than the development of resources, has expanded substantially in the post-war years. In relation to capital invested it has provided far more employment. But it rose to some extent on the backlog of demand in the first years after the

Supply-Trade and Commerce
war, and it was obviously helped by the weakness of the competition from countries still recovering from wartime devastation.
I should like to ask the minister if he would comment on that point. Not long ago I talked with a Canadian businessman just back from Europe. Whilst he shared with all of us satisfaction in the present activity of our economy, he was troubled-and he was a man of wide experience-about our competitive position in exporting manufactured goods abroad, if we look ahead three or four years. His uneasiness was based on visits he had made particularly to Germany and Switzerland. He included the United Kingdom, but it was Germany .and Switzerland that impressed him most.
He was impressed, as other people have been, with two things, notably the skill and readiness to work hard of the industrial population. He spoke about one particular piece of machinery which had been produced in and received from Germany. The purchaser compared it with a similar piece of machinery received from this continent and the advantage, he said, was all on the German side both in price and efficiency.
We have had some discussions on unemployment, and we have heard some figures Which almost took our breath away as to the way in which machines are supplanting the human element. It raises in one's mind the question of the secondary industries, which seem to be the ones where we have less success. We have less success, I take it, because they are exposed to very keen competition from the United States, with its mass production, and also because, to have the export trade they need, they have to go abroad and compete with the highly efficient European countries which are now coming back with a rush into the world markets.
With regard to the home market, of course, we have the difficulty that we cannot have it all. Some of our manufacturers feel very keenly that the share they have is not adequate. Against that, we must remember that if we do not buy abroad we cannot sell abroad. The minister has been discussing this afternoon the question of trade and especially its financial side and the side of convertibility. From the practical point of view, as far as the United Kingdom is concerned now, whilst we have not full and formal convertibility we have a practical form which works fairly well.
This question, I think, taking the long view, is a real question. I notice one writer-I think it was the same writer in the Economist -raised the question of whether the Gordon commission would find this one of the chief objectives to engage its attention, and I think


it would be very sensible if it did. There are questions being raised. I noticed a writer in the Toronto Star whom I might quote quite briefly. It seemed to me that the questions he was raising were reasonable questions. I may say this is dated June 18. He says:
Even the booming trade statistics are not quite so rosy as they appear at first glance. Exports to the U.S.-
And let me repeat that this is the Toronto Star.
-gained only 71 per cent against the 13 per cent increase with all nations, most of which already show a deficit with Canada. Further, the advance in exports to the U.S. came mainly in such low-labour content items as wood and paper products and minerals.
The rejoicing in Canadian export circles-if any-* over passage of President Eisenhower's freer trade bill was barely audible this week. The watered-down version of what the president asked originally still provides for a 5 per cent tariff cut annually over the next three years. But the bill makes it easier for U.S. industries suffering from foreign competition to gain tariff relief.
I remember being struck with a conversation I had with a very well-known American public man some years ago. I will not mention his name. This would be about 1947. He was speaking about relations between the two countries. One thing I carried away with me was this. He said: "Of course you have to face the fact in Canada that when we get agricultural surpluses here, we will take steps to protect our agricultural community." That I think has been borne out by what has happened, and it seemed to raise questions which, of course, take us back to the whole broad world picture and to GATT.
The hon. member for Eglinton has stated our attitude with regard to GATT. I think no one can deny that GATT aims at the kind of world in which we and all other people can prosper best. But it also means that the partners-and particularly the big partners- in GATT must play the game. That is only saying what has been said many times before. I shall not take the time to reiterate it. I know that representations have been made, but these problems I think exist. The sooner we grapple with them and the further ahead we can look, the less serious they will be when they catch up with us.
One thing on which the minister might be able to throw some light is this. For instance, as I have watched in Toronto what is called the golden mile and as I have watched industries going up by the score-I suppose one might say now by the hundred-there is a question that has occurred to me. The question that enters my mind is whether these are the kind of industries which are going to have to depend on export. They are consumer goods industries. They will have to depend

on the home market or on export. I wonder whether there is enough statistical material yet to be able to assess the performance of these industries. I do not know to what extent they asked or received guidance from the minister's department before they set up.
As the minister says, it is a free country and a man can do as he likes, yet most people are ready to take advice. I ask the minister if he can say anything as to the evidence to date of the capacity of these many hundreds of industries that we now have to dispose of their products and as to whether there are certain lines in which the struggle is going to be keener; whether competition is holding back some of them, and whether some of them are not yet in anything like full production. In other words, if the minister could review that situation, however generally, I think it would be of interest.
There is just one other comment I want to make, and I referred to it before. It is perfectly clear how important our home market is, and that consideration brings us back to the question of immigration. I do not know whether it is fair to ask the minister to make a comment on the government's policy on immigration but as we all know, the tide of immigration this year is flowing very slack to date. If my memory serves me aright it is about half what it was about a year ago. In any event it is much reduced. That seems to me a matter of great importance, particularly as we look ahead for a year or two.
I think that covers what I wanted to say. If the minister could comment on the matters I have raised I should be grateful.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I shall be very glad to give my views for what they are worth as to the Canadian exporter of manufactured goods being crowded out of his market. If anyone can prove that it would be impossible to manufacture here because somewhere in Europe there is a manufacturer who, because of low wages or cheaper raw material, can take our markets from us, I should like to see him do it. I say it does not happen.
I was referring to a table that was put on Hansard today by the hon. member for Eglinton. According to it, last year we exported newsprint, planks and boards, wood-pulp, aluminum and products. We are the biggest exporters of aluminum in the world. We exported nickel and products; and we are practically the only source of nickel in the world. We exported copper and products; fish and fishery products. Incidentally, that amounted to $130 million last year. We exported wheat flour. You would not think we
Supply-Trade and Commerce could export wheat flour to Europe but we do it, and we do it to something like 74 countries in the world. We export farm implements and machinery. You could say that is a highly manufactured secondary product and that it is impossible to export it, yet we did export it to the extent of $77 million last year.
Will the minister permit a comment there?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes.

The minister is referring rather to those things in which we are particularly proficient such as newsprint, and in which we have obvious advantages. As to farm machinery, it seems to me that is preeminently an industry in which for decades or even generations we have been foremost.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
That is the nature of world trade. We export the products of which we are efficient producers. There is no use attempting to export a product which is built here under handicaps. Trade is built on the fact that every nation exports the things it can best produce. That is the basis of our trade. In general, secondary industry is built to supply the Canadian market. Usually secondary industry either takes over from an import or it divides the market that is supplied by other Canadian firms.
We have never been great exporters of secondary products. We have delegations that come here-I do not say this is always so but usually it is-and point to European competition and the fact that they are competing against people whose wages are 25 per cent of ours, or perhaps 10 per cent of ours. But when you look up the trade statistics you almost invariably find that is not their real problem at all. The competition is very often from the United States, where the wages are slightly higher than they are in Canada. The electrical industry were in to see us the other day. They spoke feelingly and strongly about European competition. The figures showed that European competition was dropping, that 85 per cent of the imports came from the United States, and that about 60 per cent were imported by firms that were represented in the office. In other words, they bought components in the United States.
The market is more competitive owing to the fact that there has been a tremendous expansion of the electrical industry. I should guess that no other industry in Canada has expanded at the rate at which the electrical industry has expanded. They asserted that through European competition they are being put out of business. Yet if you take the volume of production in Canada and put

Supply-Trade and Commerce alongside it imports from Europe of electrical equipment, you will find that the latter are so minute as to be almost negligible.
Would the minister comment on one thing that has been publicized a bit?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes.
Louder.

Would the minister comment on one thing that has been publicized; that is, that in several large engineering contracts where labour enters largely into the result, Europe has been able to get the business here. Is there any truth in that?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Sometimes that is possible and sometimes not. When the hon. member compares Canada with Germany he is comparing a nation with a population of 15 million with a nation having a population of 50 million, a nation whose people have always been highly trained mechanically, who have always been efficient producers and are more so now than ever for the further reason that they are operating with new machinery and are willing to work long hours at low wages. Nevertheless we meet German competition in various places and get on all right. We export synthetic rubber to Germany, though Germany used to be the source of synthetic rubber. Now they buy rubber from Canada. So do England, France, Italy, almost every country in Europe and a few countries in the Far East.
There are commodities in respect of which Canada can compete, and those are the commodities upon which we depend for our foreign trade. A man can come along and say we cannot ship eggs into England and therefore the condition is serious, or we cannot ship butter there. It is all a matter of price. We could ship eggs and butter to England if we would sell them for the same price at which they get both from New Zealand or from across the channel on the continent. If our farmers are willing to take 43 cents a pound for butter we can sell butter abroad. That is the price recovered on the sale to Czechoslovakia. Unfortunately, however, our farmers expect to get 58 cents for butter, and they expect to get about twice the price for eggs as the price for which they sell in world trade.
There is no use moaning about that situation. We are able to sell the things we can produce efficiently, particularly metals, lumber, newsprint, and a great variety of products, and they represent Canada's export trade. I should also have mentioned wheat, oats, barley, flax and rye.
Would the minister care to comment on the textile industry?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
As to the textile industry, the condition is simple. It used to be a highly diversified industry. In other words it was made up in this country and in the United States and England of local mills that manufactured for a rather special trade. During the war the industry in the United States moved into the south. Very large units were built, and these units serve a market that can absorb very large quantities of a single item. The result is that costs are brought down through large production. The airplane has brought about speedy delivery. The result is that a dress manufacturer in Montreal, wanting a special piece of cloth that he cannot buy readily in Canada, is apt to order from the southern mills, have it shipped by airplane and receive it the next day. He finds it convenient to buy that way.
Another factor is that when new mills were constructed efficiency was also improved and the range of patterns was improved. Our industry had operated at capacity turning out war goods and supplying a market that absorbed anything the mills turned out. The result was that when slack times came they were not as far advanced toward modernization as were the mills south of the border.
Is that our chief competition?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
It is in cottons. In woollens the competition comes from the United Kingdom. In spite of the high duties on woollen goods I think we have always bought more than 50 per cent of our woollen goods from the United Kingdom. It is a highly efficient producer of woollens, due to the fact it draws on a number of markets for its wool, and also wages there are very much lower than ours. However, I am glad to say that our textile industry is recovering. We have had ups and downs in various industries throughout the years, but our industry has always had sufficient resources to enable it to become competitive again.
That is gradually happening in the textile industry, and I believe it will happen in the electrical goods industry. That industry has to reorganize. If they are being flooded with cheaper goods from somewhere else they have to see if they cannot price their goods down to meet that competition, even though it means cutting out a few frills they like to see on their products.
The only way I know to obtain an efficient economy is, when these situations occur, to allow them to be corrected through natural means. If the government went in for a short-term solution, perhaps doubling the tariff, there would be no improvement in that particular industry. We would have a sick industry on our hands forever. By letting the law of supply and demand work we keep our

industries efficient, and I maintain that Canadian industry today is efficient.

I think the minister has given me my cue to raise a particular matter. It does not fall under general discussion but has to do with the importation of electrical goods from Europe. The minister said the importation of electrical goods from Europe was practically negligible, and I am wondering if I have not perhaps laid my finger on one of the reasons for that. This matter does not come under any particular part of the government, but a question I asked was answered by an order for return from the minister's department, and it certainly has to do with the Department of Trade and Commerce.
One or two importers have written me who are largely engaged in the importation of electrical goods from Europe. I would judge from the letters I have received that the goods are manufactured in Western Germany, or perhaps in Austria. The matter has to do with the checking of the quality of goods in Europe before they are allowed to come to this side. I should not say "allowed to come to this side" because the Canadian Standards Association does not have complete power to stop goods from being imported into this country. But I claim it might almost as well have that power, because the effect of its decisions is practically the same.
The writer of the last correspondence I have had on this subject wonders if something cannot be done to expedite such inspection. He claims quite bitterly, and he is entitled to because he makes his living in this particular trade, that the approval of electrical goods manufactured in foreign countries is very slow indeed. He says the work is entrusted to what he calls a private firm. I expect that is not a good definition of the Canadian Standards Association. This organization may be private but I believe it receives from the dominion government a grant of some $20,000 a year. The minister would know and can correct me.
Apparently the function of the association is to inspect goods after they have been ordered and before they are shipped. When this man orders a consignment of electrical goods from Austria or Western Germany the goods have to be submitted for inspection. I understand there is one inspection place in Britain, probably in London, and I happen to remember the name of the other one, Arnheim, because it is a famous name in our history as well as the history of Europe. Apparently there is a good deal of red tape and delay.
Supply-Trade and Commerce
I would have been loath to believe these assertions were it not for the letters that have been written to this particular dealer by people on the other side, who are always complaining that they cannot fill these orders because they have not yet received the O.K. from the inspection point at Arnheim. This man even suggests, although I am making no such assertion, that somebody here has the power to prevent the very competition the minister has been talking about and which to some extent might account for the fact that our imports of electrical goods are negligible. Here are people, I do not know who they are or what they are, who apparently have the power-I use that word advisedly because it is proven in these letters-to hold up these shipments for an indefinite period of time. I feel it is time we should get some information upon it.
Upon the receipt of these complaints I put certain questions upon the order paper and the minister's department directed an order for return. In order to assist the minister 1 shall give the reference. It was sessional paper No. 226 of Wednesday, June 15. 1 believe I asked the logical questions. What is this association? What are its functions? Are its activities under the direct supervision of a government department? Has it branches in Europe and so on? Does it inspect, in Europe, potential imports to Canada? If so, where are such inspections made, and are such inspection points or offices open the year around so that decisions may be made without delay? What are the classes of goods with which this association deals?
Now, here is a rather vital question. Is permission to export certain goods dependent upon the result of its inspection? The answer to that is no. It is said that the customs and excise here will certainly not exercise any authority about keeping these goods out. The point is that the exporter will not send them to Canada, or perhaps I should put it the other way and say the importer will not confirm the order unless it first has the stamp of approval of this particular association.
This was all new to me, and I fancy it is new to a great many people in the country. I asked what was the source of the funds necessary to carry on its operations? I have outlined some of the questions, but I am not going to weary the house by any full recital of the answers. As I say, they are already registered with the parliamentary papers branch so that he who runs may read.
I was interested in the answer to question No. 8, to the effect that the association does not have any mandatory powers in regard
6152	HOUSE OF
Supply-Trade and Commerce to granting permission to export or even import goods. According to the complaints from these business firms, time and time again they are based on delay. Time and time again my constituents tell me these goods have been held up for as long as two years. These letters say that it seems rather ridiculous to question goods which pass very freely to other countries, and mention is made of Australia and one or two other commonwealth countries with which no difficulty is experienced. However, they have considerable difficulty when it comes to passing the Canadian Standards Association.
As I say, my friend goes further and suggests that here is an opportunity where there may be some rather illegitimate work, where it might be of interest to certain people not to have these goods imported into Canada. This might be an avenue for some such thing. As I say, I make no such assertion. I think it is a matter upon which we might get some information and have it cleared up.
I have talked at greater length than I intended, but in order that we may have the whole picture, and since I cannot quote these letters, I may say a word about what they contain. One complainant says he knows that vacuum cleaners cannot be sold in Canada without this Canadian Standards Association approval. He says their apparatus has already been approved by many associations in other countries, and he has prepared the necessary steps for approval in Canada but without success. Another complainant, a different firm, say they have paid the fees demanded and now hope they will receive the approval for which they have been waiting for the last two years. Another comments that it is ridiculous that the sale of these implements continues in Europe and commonwealth countries, while we cannot get permission, except over a long period, to sell in Canada.
This last one rather alarmed me and caused me to feel that while the man's suspicions probably were completely wrong it would be better to have this thing cleaned up so these suspicions could not exist. In a letter dated Arnheim, January 21, 1955, this appears:
We feel that it is necessary that our-
I do not intend to use the name.
-has to go once more to Arnheim in order to look after the "red tape".
The words red tape are in quotation marks. That is important because I am not making any accusation against anyone but I think there is a situation that the public and this house ought to know something about. I did talk to some of the officials in the department of customs and excise. Quite frankly


they did not know about it. They knew about the association, and they knew vaguely what its functions were. But they did not know what was going on. They did give me this piece of information, that they certainly did not prevent goods from coming from Europe without the approval of this association. As I say, in my opinion it seems to work the same way.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
The Canadian Standards Association, Mr. Chairman, is an association of Canadian businessmen. Various firms can become members. The president of the association this year is the dean of engineering at McGill University. The national research council also has always worked closely with the Canadian Standards Association. It is the final authority on quality that is recognized by every Canadian manufacturer. In Ontario it is illegal to instal any electrical apparatus that has not been approved by the Canadian Standards Association. I believe that provincial laws in other provinces cover the same ground. It is not a federal service, although the federal government regards it as so valuable that it contributes $20,000 a year to its budget. It sponsors the various meetings of industries and fixes standards for industries.
After the war years Britain complained that there was too much delay in getting approval from the Canadian Standards Association for goods from that country, and asked that a branch of the association be established there. I called in the association and they readily agreed to establish a branch in England. I think it is in Manchester, if I am not mistaken; in one of the industrial towns of England. A very efficient branch of the association is maintained there and a final inspection is given in England of British goods.
This return says London.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Perhaps it is London, but I thought it was in one of the midland cities. Then later we received a request to establish a branch of the association on the continent. As my hon. friend says, a branch was established in Holland at Arnheim. It is all very well to say there are delays in getting inspection, but the delay probably comes about if the quality is not up to Canadian standards. I think it is tremendously important to the Canadian people and to Canadian manufacturers that goods imported here are up to Canadian standards of manufacture. There are difficulties about imports, but often the import is of cheap material. I feel that the Canadian Standards Association stands between the Canadian people and the quality of the goods sold to

them over the counters in our shops. I think it is a most valuable service.
I must say it has always been maintained on a very high plane. The people who run the affairs of the association are not strictly commercial people. As I say, they went to McGill University and got their president this year. Last year I believe he was a retired steel manufacturer. But I can assure my hon. friend with pleasure that it is a first class organization. Its purpose is to give a satisfactory and a prompt service to those who are willing to pay for it, and I can say that its fees are moderate. It simply operates more or less on a cost basis. I am sure when my hon. friend looks into the matter further he will find no ground for undue criticism.

Mr. Chairman, may I speak on the same subject brought up by the hon. member for Saskatoon. As a matter of fact what I shall say, I believe, will point up the fact that there are certainly very wide differences of opinion among business people in Canada today on this particular topic. Of course it may be only a part of a much larger problem. If I were directing my remarks in any particular direction, I might say that I believe businessmen would be very happy if a specific part of the Department of Trade and Commerce were allotted liaison duties between businessmen and various other government departments. I refer specifically, of course, to the problems which arise when letters go from the Department of Trade and Commerce to the Department of National Revenue, or the reverse.
These are natural problems which are bound to arise. However, they also make businessmen prone to believe that at times they are not treated justly. As a matter of fact, while the minister was in Australia and New Zealand I had a problem in connection with the importation of vacuum bottles from Japan. I was amazed at the number of letters that passed back and forth before we were able to arrive at a fairly satisfactory solution to the problem.
This problem of the Canadian Standards Association is another one of a similar nature. As the last speaker said, it is difficult to find out just exactly what the situation is in connection with the association, or to ascertain its official status. I notice that in their general information they indicate that the Canadian Standards Association is a non-profit, non-government standards development organization. It was incorporated by dominion charter in 1919 and by supplementary letters patent granted in April of 1944.
The average person would assume that it had no connection whatsoever with any branch of government. Yet if one will look at 50433-389
Supply-Trade and Commerce page 35 of the Ottawa telephone directory he will find the Canadian Standards Association listed under the telephone number 2-8211 of the government of Canada. And if one goes to the official telephone directory issued by the government he finds the Canadian Standards Association listed at page 8. So I assume we must give this association some kind of semi-official status, and we must ask that some recognition of that fact be given by the various government departments.
The problem about which I should like to speak is diametrically opposed to the problem raised by the hon. member for Saskatoon. A large part of the electrical industry in Canada today is complaining that goods are being imported into this country which do not meet the standards set up by this association. As a matter of fact appeals have been made not only to the Minister of Trade and Commerce but also to the Minister of National Revenue.
I believe the answers received from both of them are legally quite correct. But the fact that some liaison is required to clear up problems of this kind is pointed up in this instance. I do not think one can say to the businessman, "This association is entirely outside the government. Even though we list it in the telephone directory and in our own government directory, it is outside." I do not think the government can say, "This association sets the standards from one end of this country to the other, but it is not our responsibility to see that those standards are observed."
There are nine or ten individual authorities from one end of the country to the other, including those in hydroelectric activities, which must assert the rights and protect the interests of Canadian manufacturers. But obviously it is too big a job, and cannot be done that way. If we are faced with the problem that as these standards cross from one provincial boundary to another they reach a point where they are not recognized at all, then I say it is time we put this matter on the agenda for the next dominion-provincial conference. Certainly we should be looking toward some solution of the problem.
I would read from bulletin 68 issued by the Canadian Lamp and Fixture Manufacturers Association, Incorporated. This bulletin is headed with the words "Buck-passing Deluxe" and states:
The present government set-up with respect to our request for a declaration on all MA forms-
I suppose that refers to customs entry-forms:
-provides them with the best opportunity of buckpassing seen anywhere. Our letters and telegrams
6154	HOUSE OF
Supply-Trade and Commerce to the Minister of Trade and Commerce and to the Department of National Revenue, all result in having them remind us that they cannot do anything, because it is not their responsibility. The various government departments, instead of being co-ordinating units, each seem to have jurisdiction over only a part of a law, which allows them to say, it's not our baby.
I go along with the argument that the federal government should devise a plan whereby, upon the entry of electrical goods from a foreign country, certain standards must be maintained. The request is made that an affidavit or declaration be attached to prove that the article imported meets with the safety standards of the Canadian Standards Association. In bulletin 68 they go on to say:
But we will be told, you can't do that, you will be interfering with the rights of the provinces under the BNA Act. To which I would say, that this is a matter of public safety and is a federal responsibility, in the same manner that we have laws affecting the manufacture and sale of food, drugs and possibly other products. Defective wiring of electrical goods including lamps and lighting fixtures, can create a hazard that is dangerous to life and property. While the BNA Act may have been a good instrument when it was written at confederation eighty-eight years ago, it has since become one of the means of dividing the country into ten provinces instead of one Canada.
I am sure we will not all subscribe to the last sentence in the brief, but what the association is pointing out is that the safety of the people is involved. Importation of goods adversely affecting the health and safety of the people is not allowed. Why should we allow the importation of manufactured articles of this kind which do not meet the standards set by our own Canadian Standards Association?
This is another problem which is not tied up with tariffs or with GATT in any way. I am wondering what the government is going to do for our manufacturers in this connection.
I am not asking for tariff protection or an import quota, but I do point out that the government ask us to compete with goods entering Canada but which do not come up to the standards with which, by law, we must comply.
Let me illustrate the point. Here are two lamps, almost identical. One is marked "A" and the other is marked "B". Lamp "A" is manufactured with materials which are quite satisfactory in the United States. Lamp "B" is manufactured with materials which meet the standards set by the Canadian Standards Association. Right on lamp "B" is stamped the approval of the Canadian Standards Association. That is stamped right on the socket. What is the manufacturer in Canada up against? First of all, the socket in this lamp costs 6J cents more than the socket in the other lamp. That is, the socket of


the Canadian lamp as distinct from the lamp manufactured to United States standards costs that much more. The cord set on the Canadian lamp costs cents more than the United States lamp. The label itself costs 1 cent. In order to obtain this approval it costs the manufacturer $15 per annum. If he produces a new line of lamps of this type then it is necessary for him to open a new file with the standards association and pay them $130. That is a deposit, it is true, but the minimum that is required in any type of operation of this kind is at least $50.
I am reliably informed that in the lamp industry in Canada there have been approximately 2,500 lay-offs. This should be their busy time. The summertime, when they are getting prepared for the winter business, the gift business later in the year, should be their busy time. These articles are being brought in and placed on sale in the various department stores. The average individual is certainly not going to go around and examine these different articles to see whether these special stamps mean anything to him. As a result, there is a large volume of this type of equipment coming into the country and being sold through retail store outlets. We can say there is a plan to overcome it, but obviously no jurisdiction in Canada would have enough people to run around to individual stores to prevent the sale of unapproved merchandise. The logical answer would seem to be some type of protection at the border which would ensure that this type of article did not come across, unless it was indicated at the time that it met the standards set up by the Canadian Standards Association.
In dealing with this, I say we are dealing with a problem that confronts businessmen in connection with many of their operations. I repeat, the problems do not involve the question of getting out of the GATT agreement or raising the tariff. There are many problems that confront them every day in the week, problems that involve their coming to Ottawa to discuss methods of overcoming those obstructions to being able to market on fair and equal terms with the imported products from other countries.
That is why I said I should like to see here some specific place where they could come and say, "Now, here is a problem we have. I do not know whether it involves the Department of National Revenue or trade and commerce, but we would like to lay it down here to see if we cannot put the thing together without the cross-fire of letters from one department to the other".

The Minister of National Revenue and I have got along very well in many matters involving customs. I am thinking of items like having an article declared "of a class or kind manufactured in Canada". But it is sometimes several months before the impetus originally generated to get this type of declaration through the Department of National Revenue is brought to fulfilment. I have companies in my own constituency such as the Brydon Brass Manufacturing Company Limited, who are gradually becoming able to build products in Canada which, so far as we are concerned, were formerly manufactured only in the United States. Yet there has always been a considerable lapse of time before they were able to put themselves in the position to which they are entitled under the rules of the Department of National Revenue.
Further, there is the firm of Wilson and Cousins, which is also located in my constituency. We have had some correspondence on that company to get across to the department the fact that it is only a question of terminology as to whether an article is processed fully before it comes into the country or whether it is only semi-processed. That makes a good deal of difference in the ability to continue to manufacture and do a good job in connection with the lines they are manufacturing here. So once again I say, let us see whether we cannot, within the framework of the Department of Trade and Commerce, establish some place where these various problems such as "of a class or kind made in Canada", or problems such as C.S.A. approval can be funnelled through and some assistance obtained. I am thinking back to an editorial that appeared in the Quebec Chronicle-Telegraph, dated March 19, 1955. I quote part of the editorial:
Why not give serious thought to increasing production of the things to which our raw materials contribute? For the most part, we have the manufacturing facilities. Why not convert the raw materials at home, and export the finished product? The facilities are here, likewise the manpower and the electrical energy required. There is little justification in missing out on the gains to the country through this industrial effort.
Here is a method of assistance which will enable us to get into the secondary line of business and really promote Canadian trade. Therefore I am thankful to the hon. member for Saskatoon. His problem with the C.S.A. may be different. I only hope that any article which is imported into Canada will have to be manufactured to the standards we accept here for the safety of the people of this country.

In view of the fact that the minister undoubtedly has been impressed with the impetus of wheat this afternoon, I want to remind him-probably he does not need to be reminded-that there are other areas in Canada which are interested in sterling as well as the wheat-producing areas of western Canada.
I happen to come from an area which at one time was dependent upon the sterling market almost entirely. Our whole product, the apple crop in the Annapolis valley, was sold in the British market. At one time we exported more apples to Great Britain than did all the rest of the British commonwealth put together. Owing to circumstances over which no particular government has had absolute control, the situation has changed so that for some time we sold none. Last year we did sell a relatively few boxes of apples.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: All you had.
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: At a cost to the Canadian government.

It was a substantial part of what we had last year. I will admit that owing to the devastation caused by "Hurricane Edna" which stripped the apple trees for us, our crop was not large. If it had not been for Edna's visitation we would have had many more apples to sell to Great Britain. That is not the situation this year. I am glad the minister reminds us of the fact that we did not have too many last year. I am reminding him of the fact that, according to current indications, we are going to have many more apples this year. In fact it will be the largest crop we have had since the reconversion following the war.
Every possible opportunity which may be open to us to enlarge our market in Great Britain will be not only welcomed but waited for most anxiously by the growers in the Annapolis valley. I have on my file letters from various purchasers in Great Britain last year praising us because of the condition of our product. The minister knows, and particularly the Minister of Agriculture knows, our export was entirely of the culinary variety, the barrel pack, though relatively low-grade, for cooking purposes. The dessert variety would compare favourably with any produced anywhere in the world. I have letters from various importers in Great Britain praising them and saying they would like to buy more this year if they were available.
I know there are difficulties in the way. I see reports sometimes of convertibility being
6156	HOUSE OF
Supply-Trade and Commerce around the corner. I know that when convertibility comes, if it ever comes, it will come one minute after midnight one day, and no one will know about it until it breaks, and naturally so. But last year an arrangement was worked out whereby $2,500,000 was made available for the purchase of Canadian apples, a certain proportion for Nova Scotia and a larger proportion for British Columbia. This year, with a larger crop, I hope some arrangement can be made to the same end.
My hon. friend from York West spoke of the difficulties in regard to exports. I read in the British newspapers that they are concerned with the difficulties they encounter in exporting their products to the Canadian market. We have difficulties in exporting our agricultural products there at least. There is almost a 100 per cent tariff which the British producer enjoys in selling his products in the local market. I understand the purchasing value of the shilling internally is almost the same as it was before, and it gives the producer there a tremendous advantage.
I can imagine there are pressure groups in that country who would welcome a continuation of the status quo. But surely there must be some ways and means whereby our two .governments, working together, can accommodate each other to increase the flow of goods back and forth between the two countries, and so produce the happy result that there can be more sterling available than there has been heretofore. It was and still is one of the great traditional markets of eastern Canada.
The minister should keep one eye on the West Indies market and the making available of more sterling for the purchase of Canadian goods there. That would go a long way toward helping the producers of the maritime provinces. I simply wanted to put this on record, because there has been a good deal of emphasis on wheat, and I suppose there will be more before the day is over. I wanted to put the claims of eastern Canada at least in proper perspective.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I may say that we are well aware that the apple growers usually sell their apples. They always have sold their apples since I have been in the government, and I am sure they will do so next year. In fact we have quite encouraging messages from England on the subject.

Mr. Chairman, I simply want to support the remarks made by the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings with respect to trade with Great Britain, but I want them to relate to British Columbia apples. I was very pleased to hear the minister's encouraging remarks.

Mr. Chairman, before this item is passed, I wonder if the minister would care to give us a little more information regarding the possibility of an all-Canadian pipe line than was given by the Prime Minister when I asked him a question on that subject a few days ago. He simply told us there were three propositions being considered, that the government liked proposition one, hoped that if they could not get that proposition they would get proposition two, and hoped they would not have to fall back on proposition three. That is very indefinite. This is not a matter of defence, that there should be so much secrecy about it.
While the minister is answering that question, will he tell us whether consideration has been given to the government subsidizing a private company in this respect, or whether the government has given any study to the possibility of a publicly-owned pipe line being built in conjunction with the provincial governments and hydro departments?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am unable to throw any light on the pipe-line situation other than to say that every possibility is being studied, and studied intensively.
I hope a solution can be announced before long, but I cannot announce it today. My hon. friend has the advantage of me if he knows what propositions one, two and three are; I do not.
I do not.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Well, we are even on that.

I should like to have the minister's comment on two points. The minister will unquestionably agree that the marketing of wheat is one of the most important problems in this country. He is also aware that the sale of wheat is in the hands of some half dozen international grain firms. There are two firms in particular, Dreyfuss-Bumge in France and Continental Grain in Belgium. There is at the present time no Canadian firm or any firm interested in the selling of Canadian wheat particularly. These international firms, of course, are no more interested in the selling of Canadian wheat than they are in the sale of French, Argentine or any other wheat. It was not always thus. We did have grain exporters in this country in days gone by. Would the minister care to say why we do not have them now?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Perhaps I could answer this question now. We do have them now. James Richardson and Sons have handled several export transactions, and there are other firms. Northern Sales are

handling the Polish deal and have handled a number of export sales of Canadian wheat. Dreyfuss-Bunge and Continental are, of course, the great international traders who have been in business ever since I have known anything about wheat, which goes back a good many years. They are very able dealers, and well established in every country in the world.
They are not interested in selling Canadian wheat.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: No exporter is interested in what wheat he sells. All he is interested in is making a sale. He sells what the customer wants to buy. The selling is done by other agencies; the wheat board has agencies around the world, and the Canadian government has trade commissioners around the world. The dealers are simply the people who take the wheat in store at Fort William, transport it to Montreal, load it on a ship, charter the tonnage and guarantee delivery to the customer. If they hear of a trade they try to work out a deal to sell whatever wheat they can to the customer.
Is it not a fact that these arrangements are usually made through the international grain firms like Dreyfuss-Bunge and Continental?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Not necessarily. They probably handle half the world's trade in wheat, but I doubt if it is much more than half. There are United States firms that do the same thing.

There is one other point. In reading some statistics in the commercial letter of the Canadian Bank of Commerce of June, 1955, I notice that for the three months from January to March inclusive in 1955 Canada exported $177-9 million of agricultural and vegetable products. In the same period Canada imported $118-7 million of the same products. I should like to ask the minister why in his opinion it is necessary for Canada, an agricultural country, to import $118 million-odd of agricultural products in three months.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I suppose the reason is that people like to have it. Our people are getting more and more into the habit of eating strawberries in February and fresh vegetables in every month of the year.
The hon. member was talking about the importation of agricultural products into Canada in the months of January, February and March. If he would talk to me about July, August and September that would be Canada's time. If we were importing heavily
Supply-Trade and Commerce in that period I would worry about it. He asks why it is necessary. It is not necessary. We could stop our people from eating oranges and grapefruit in the winter and say they cannot have vegetables unless they get them out of the deep freeze. But this being a free country, we let people do as they like.
Does the minister suggest that the products he referred to account for the sum total of $118 million?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Oh, yes.
