speechtext:
AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Chairman, my position with respect to the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce is about the same as last year. I objected then to the serious trade situation, and pointed out that there was danger because all our eggs had been concentrated in one basket in the United States and we had not been able to make much improvement so far as our trade with the United Kingdom was concerned. The hon. member for Eglinton and others have pointed this out today in very clear fashion, and the committee will be spared my remarks in this respect. However, I have one particular point in mind that refers to two or three branches of the department which I feel involves policy, and I wish to mention it briefly. It is not a new matter, it has been mentioned many times in the house and elsewhere.
I refer to the growing trend for Canada's imports and exports to move through United States ports rather than Canadian ports. This has been mentioned by many members in the past. I referred to it in the throne speech debate this year, but I think the matter has reached a serious stage and some consideration and attention must be given to it by the department. There is a growing trend for manufactured products shipped out of the country and goods shipped into our country to move through United States rather than Canadian ports and, to make the matter more serious, there is the fact that a good proportion of the goods going out of the country come from our protected industries.
I wish I could say this evening that the department has done something in this regard. I am afraid I cannot even report that they have done nothing. I think they have made

Supply-Trade and Commerce the situation worse, and there are three good examples which I wish to put before the department for its consideration. First of all, when one considers a matter such as this one naturally thinks of what the publications, reports and periodicals have to say about it. Are we really trying to promote the use of Canadian ports? I have always followed Foreign Trade, a periodical put out by the Department of Trade and Commerce, and I must say I was just about floored by a series of articles I found in it.
In the issues of November 27, December 11 and December 25, 1954, there is a series of interesting articles with respect to the trade situation under the heading, "How to Sell Through New York". I would point out that it does not say "How to sell in New York", but "How to Sell through New York". I ask hon. members what is going on in the department. We are supposed to be promoting Canadian ports, yet I pick up that article and I am confronted by that title.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Did you read the article?

I have read the article and I admit that it explains the situation later. It points out that the export-import facilities of New York are available to Canadian exporters and importers, but after all we either have to get into the trade business or get out of it, and we have to stand on our own feet. Such a series of articles would create a tremendous amount of criticism everywhere, and you can just imagine the reaction to them. Our exporters and importers use the facilities at New York, and what happens? The first thing you know they are using the port of New York. That is the point I am making this evening.
Then there comes to my mind the fact, and I have checked it as best I can, that our sellers, promoters and advertisers abroad are not doing the best they can to promote the shipment of goods to and from Canada through Canadian ports. I refer specifically to the trade commissioner service. The people down home have taken up the matter with the department. They have made inquiries and have also checked with the commissioners when they have been in our part of the country. The answers to our inquiries all bear out the fact that our trade commissioners overseas have never received any instructions to promote shipping through Canadian ports in all their efforts to obtain business overseas.
I feel that our trade commissioners and others who are trying to promote Canadian trade should definitely be instructed along the same lines as United States trade commissioners. They should be told to go out and

almost insist that the business be done through these ports on which we are now spending so much money for purposes of development.
There is also the fact that contrasting figures with respect to the value and tonnage of shipments of goods through Canadian and United States ports are available only to a limited degree. I should like to refer to a question of the hon. member for Royal having to do with the point I am trying to make this evening, which was answered on March 21, 1955. The question is found at page 2215 of Hansard and is as follows:
1.	What was the amount (a) in tons; (b) in value of goods manufactured or produced in Canada exported through Canadian seaports and United States seaports, respectively, for each month from January 1, 1954 to February 1, 1955?
2.	What was the amount (a) in tons; (b) in value of goods imported for use in Canada through Canadian and United States seaports, respectively, for each month from January 1, 1954 to February 1, 1955?
The answer is the enlightening thing here. It reads:
1.	Records of Canadian exports through Canadian seaports and United States seaports are not maintained on a monthly basis but are compiled annually only. The compilation of this information for the calendar year 1954 will not be completed until about April 15, 1955. Tonnage figures are not available.
2.	(a) Amount in tons is not recorded.
Then the answer is given to question 2 (b). The point I am trying to make is that it should be possible, and I do not see why it is not, to have a complete record with respect to these figures. I may be wrong, but I understand that the United States make available all tonnage and value figures with respect to goods passing through their ports, and we are entitled to have the exact information. People down my way have asked the minister and his department at various times why these figures are not available, and of course the department has not been able to answer them. They think there is something that is being held back with respect to these figures.
It could be that the figures are not startling. The only evidence we have, though, Mr. Chairman, indicates that the figures are not good. The figures that are given in reply to part 2 (b) of the question of the hon. member for Royal shows that roughly one-third of the goods imported into Canada through Canadian and United States seaports go through United States ports. I am speaking very roughly, Mr. Chairman.
It is a rather sorry state of affairs when goods have to go through United States ports to come into Canada. I ask everyone here how much United States goods are now entering the United States through Canadian ports. I would bet that the amount was very small, if there are any. There are other

figures that have been mentioned. I admit I do not have proof here but we calculate, particularly in so far as these protected industries are concerned such as whisky and automobiles, that only one-seventh of the exports of those industries are going through Canadian ports. They are going through New York and the other United States seaports.
I do say it is a serious state of affairs, and we are entitled to all the figures. Those figures must be made available. I suggest that when they are made available we can assess the situation. If what I say is correct, then let us do something about it and really get into this business.
In closing I should like to review the situation. I have said we are worried. We are seriously worried in the maritimes and other areas where the seaports are the lifeblood of the community. We feel that every action should be taken to ensure that Canadian goods both leaving and entering Canada are sent through a Canadian port. We say that above all the products of the protected industries should go through these Canadian ports; we should almost insist upon that.
Then I used a periodical, which I do not believe

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: You misused the periodical. You know very well to what that article referred.

I am pointing out that the headline on that article, "How to Sell through New York" to my mind is not in keeping with a concentrated effort to see that Canadian ports are used. I will admit that the minister has a point. I will admit that we have had articles on the port of Saint John and I presume on Halifax and Montreal in that same periodical. It is a good one, and I enjoy reading it. But I do say it seems peculiar that a Canadian periodical like this should be trying to sell New York generally.
I pointed that out, and I said that the salesmanship of the department, in instances like that, does not seem to be consistent. Then I mentioned that our advertisers abroad, those people who are trying to sell Canada and Canadians, to my knowledge do not have complete instructions to sell, and almost insist, that Canadian ports be used in the various transactions.
I realize that you cannot tell the buyers overseas that they have to use Canadian ports. But I do say that some long-range program of salesmanship should be given to these trade commissioners. I mentioned the fact that these figures with respect to tonnages
Supply-Trade and Commerce and values of goods moving through Canadian and United States ports should definitely be made available.
I feel that this is a very serious matter. It has been bandied about for two or three years. The Canadian Manufacturers Association and other people who are vitally interested in this matter, such as boards of trade throughout the country, have all brought in resolutions; the matter has been talked about and it has been presented to the department, but I honestly cannot say that I feel the department is making a serious effort in this regard.
We all realize that there must be an effort made for Canadian trade abroad. I am reminded that Mr. Coyne said recently that international trade is losing its importance. If that is true, then I suppose we should not be worried about that. This statement appeared in the Montreal Gazette on May 6, 1955. I do not believe that. I think that Canada's future is in the trading world.
In that same connection I refer to a statement that was made by a certain economist from Britain who was here this year at the University of Western Ontario. He said Canada is unknown as a world manufacturer. That is the opinion of one man who has been in close touch with this matter in Great Britain. He says we are unknown overseas. I have tried to develop the point that our goods are not being sold over there. I say that in our plans to sell Canadian goods we have to try to insist that our ports are used.
I shall leave it at that, Mr. Chairman. I simply say we have spent a great deal of money on our Canadian ports. They are fine ports. The men who man the ships and the men who work the cargoes in these ports are good. They deserve a good living in Canada. In my opinion our system and our whole plan does not seem to be consistent. Definite efforts must be made to see that when Canadian goods come into the country or when they are leaving the country, they pass through Canadian ports.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
This is, to my mind, definitely a speech without any substance. As a matter of fact, under Liberal trade policies the maritime ports have enjoyed the greatest movement of tonnage in their history during the last 12 months. The same magazine to which my hon. friend referred has published articles on shipping through Canadian ports, whereas the same information it gave about New York referred to that city as a trading centre.
The hon. member's reference to New York was, of course, part of the Tory campaign

Supply-Trade and Commerce against trade with the United States. That trade is no good; it is dangerous. The fact of the matter is that New York is the greatest distributing centre on the eastern seaboard. In Canada it is customary to sell goods through New York for distribution from there; that is the purpose of that article, as my friend very well knows unless he is boasting when he says he read the article and, in fact, he only read the headline. I think if we are going to have anything serious in this debate we ought to put a stop to that kind of nonsense being talked in this house.

This evening, I should like to place three or four questions before the minister with regard to the construction of a natural gas pipe line from Alberta to Ontario and Quebec. In order to give the background for my questions I shall have to review shortly some of the events that have taken place. As the minister knows, in 1953 he announced government policy with regard to the piping of natural gas.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: There is nothing in the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce having to do with the piping of natural gas, and I do not propose to answer any questions.
Well, now, Mr. Chairman, the minister has already answered questions this afternoon having to do with natural gas.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That was this afternoon.
This comes under the minister's department-

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: It does not.

-because licences for the exportation of gas come under one branch of his department. I forget which branch it is. In any event it is a question of the exportation of gas, oil and power, which are under the jurisdiction of the minister in his capacity as Minister of Trade and Commerce.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The department considers those problems when they are placed before it, and not before.

For that reason I am proposing to ask the minister these questions. If the minister does not wish to answer, or if he refuses to answer, that of course is his responsibility. But I am rather surprised that-

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: You can be surprised all you like. You can't surprise me. I have known you for 20 years.

I am rather surprised that the minister should lose his temper when we are in the course of a discussion of his estimates


which is entirely in order. It shows only too clearly the dictatorial attitude this minister has adopted, and his contempt for parliamentary procedure. If this minister is going to treat parliament and the affairs of parliament in this contemptuous way, then I say to him it is time he went to the Senate.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. If I understood the hon. member correctly, he has stated that the minister was treating parliament with contempt. In my opinion that is unparliamentary and should be withdrawn.

Well, I always withdraw when I am asked to withdraw by the Chair. But I do say that the minister has stated, without hearing my question at all, that he refuses to answer it. Whether or not that is contempt of parliament I shall leave to the Chair to decide.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. Perhaps the hon. member would allow me to rise at this time to indicate that there is some difficulty in connection with the matter he is attempting to raise. We are dealing with the first item of the Department of Trade and Commerce. The custom has grown up in recent years of allowing a fairly wide debate on the first item. May I point out to the hon. member that that is merely the custom and that according to our rule, which has not been changed, standing order 58(2) states that speeches in committee of the whole house must be strictly relevant to the item or clause under consideration.
If I apply the rule, then of course the hon. member is out of order in discussing a pipe line under this item. If I follow the custom, the hon. member is entitled to discuss in a general way the administration of the Department of Trade and Commerce. As I understand it, that is what has taken place earlier in the debate. I feel that perhaps the hon. member should think twice before he attempts to make a speech on a pipe line matter at this time. There are occasions in the house and in committee when such matters may be discussed most properly.
I feel that in accordance with our custom this is the appropriate time to discuss the administration of the Department of Trade and Commerce, but not to discuss a particular matter such as the pipe line which the hon. member has indicated he wishes to discuss.

Mr. Chairman, may I point out that on the administration item of a department we are entitled to discuss the various matters which come under that department. Under the rules that is in order; and furthermore-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. If the hon. member wishes to tell me that he is in order, under the rules, then I would appreciate it very much if he would refer to the rule to which he wishes to draw my attention. I have referred to standing order 58(2). If the hon. member has some rule or some standing order to which he can direct my attention and upon which he bases his assertion, I would be glad to hear it.

The whole discussion this
afternoon has been on particular aspects of the Department of Trade and Commerce. That was true also of the discussion of the first item in the estimates of all departments which have been before us.
I would point out that I have here the annual report of the Department of Trade and Commerce for the calendar year 1954, and that one branch of that department is known as the standards branch. I now quote from that portion of the report which bears the subheading "Electricity and Fluid Exportation Act", and which says:
This act prohibits the export from Canada, without a licence, of electrical energy or piped fluids, which include natural gas. Five additional licences, one relating to small quantities of surplus electricity (renewed after discontinuance of a year) and four relating to crude oil, were issued in 1954.
The volume of natural gas exported during the year was somewhat lower than in the previous year for the two exporting companies. All gas exports are in accordance with authorizations of the petroleum and natural gas conservation board of Alberta, and the federal government. A third licensee has still to obtain permission of United States authorities to import into that country.
Oil exports continued via the Interprovincial Pipe Line Company's pipe line.
I am proposing now to ask the minister three cr four questions concerning the policy of his department-which means the policy of the government-with regard to the export of gas. The minister himself, as Minister of Trade and Commerce, laid down government policy on March 13, 1953, and I would refer hon. members in that connection to page 2930 of Hansard for that year. In making his statement the minister quoted a letter he had written to Premier Manning of Alberta. The letter is dated January 2, 1953, and two paragraphs from it are as follows:
We had a conversation about this subject-
He is referring to the export of natural gas. -at Sarnia, when Premier Frost was present. At that time, I stated that gas from Alberta must be available to potential customers in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, and in the intervening provinces, before further export of gas could be authorized. This attitude is consistent with the position that the government has taken with regard to the export of hydroelectric power for many years. You will appreciate that the supply of gas through a pipe line is analogous with the supply of electric power, in that both demand continuity of supply.
Supply-Trade and Commerce I am aware that, for the period when natural gas is first made available in Ontario and Quebec, and until the load can be built up, such a pipeline project is unlikely to be profitable, either for the producers of gas or for the owners of the pipe line. Nevertheless, there is evidence that a pipeline project for Ontario and Quebec can be worked out and that the project will be profitable over a period of years.
After quoting the letter the minister went on to say:
This letter is of course consistent with the government policy I have outlined.
Earlier in his speech, as reported at page 2929 of Hansard, the minister outlined policy as follows:
Therefore the policy of the government of Canada is to refuse permits for moving natural gas by pipe line across an international boundary until such time as we are convinced that there can be no economic use, present or future, for that natural gas within Canada.
Then I go back again to the part of his speech which followed the quoting of the letter to Mr. Manning:
While the government of Alberta has proposals before it which involve the movement of gas eastward and across the United States border to Minneapolis, or through the United States to southern Ontario, permits to that end will not be granted under the terms of the Electricity and Fluid Exportation Act. This government has reason to believe that it is economically feasible to build a gas pipe line from southern Alberta to Toronto and Montreal, serving the intervening Canadian cities, and government policy will require that Canadian gas be used in Canada accordingly.
That was in March of 1953. On April 2 of the following year the minister appeared before the standing committee of the house on railways, canals and telegraph lines. That was about a year after he had announced policy. He gave evidence during the discussion of a bill to incorporate a company known as Niagara Gas Transmission Limited. This is what he had to say then. I am quoting from page 79 of the proceedings of that committee:

Mr. Chairman, the policy of the government has been laid down, that no gas can be exported from Canada unless the present and foreseeable needs of Canada are first taken care of. Now there is a certain capacity of pipe line to be built from the west to Toronto, and in order to finance that line there will have to be quantities of gas dedicated to that particular line, as I understand it. Is that correct, Mr. Milner?
Mr. Milner was the vice-president of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited.
Yes, sir.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
No, there has been no change in government policy in that regard.
Then he was asked again by the Leader of the Opposition on April 5, and I quote his answer from page 2705 of Hansard:
Mr. Speaker, there is nothing new that I could place before the house at this time. The gentlemen who are interested in the establishment of a pipe line in Canada to bring the gas from the west to the east are, I understand, still persisting in their efforts to work out arrangements for the private financing of that project. The government's policy with respect to gas is unchanged and remains such as was stated on March 13, 1953.
Newspaper reports persisted that there might be a change in government policy and that there were other schemes, and on April 26 I asked a question of the Minister of Public Works, who was on that date the Acting Minister of Trade and Commerce. The question was asked because Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited, which is the chosen instrument for building the line across Canada, was making an application to the board of transport commissioners either that day or the following day. The question and answer will be found at page 3163 of Hansard. I asked:
Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Acting Minister of Trade and Commerce. A press dispatch this morning indicates the probability that 

Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited will be buying the gas distribution and manufacturing system in the city of Montreal from the Quebec hydro. Could the minister tell the house whether government policy still remains as announced on March 13, 1953, and confirmed by the Prime Minister on March 18 of this year and again on April 5? As the minister knows, that announcement was to the effect that Canadian needs for natural gas must be met first before export is permitted. Would the minister also say whether there has been any change in the policy of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines in this regard?
I included that in my question because there were rumours that Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited was trying to get out of its obligation to build an all-Canadian line. Here was the answer by Hon. Mr. Winters:
Mr. Speaker, to the best of my knowledge the answer to both questions would be in the negative. There has been no change in government policy in regard to the exportation of fuel, and as I understand it there has been no change in the policy of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited.
I believe that Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited went before the board of transport commissioners and got an order giving an extension of time, on the statement that they were going to build an all-Canadian line. As a matter of fact I think the Minister of Trade and Commerce and I are pretty close together on this whole question. There has been no quarrel-

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I am worried now.

The first thing we know, Mr. Chairman, he will be withdrawing what he said about me a few moments ago. There has never been any dispute over the fact that there could be a branch line down to Minneapolis. But the main pipe line had to be laid in Canadian soil.
After this hearing before the board of transport commissioners in April, we began to read reports in the press that Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited was no longer planning to build an all-Canadian route, but that it was negotiating with a very large United States company known as Tennessee Gas Transmission Company for a new set-up under which Alberta gas would go down into the cities of Minneapolis and Chicago and into Pennsylvania, and Ontario and Quebec would get United States gas rather than Canadian gas.
The Prime Minister was asked a question again six days ago, on July 8, by the hon. member for York South, who had received a wire from the mayors of Fort William and Port Arthur protesting any plan which would delay the construction of an all-Canadian line. He asked the Prime Minister to bring the house up to date on the present situation. Here was the reply:
There are three alternatives that are being very carefully investigated and about which, of course, the commitments of many different interests are

required. There is one that we prefer to the other two. There is a third that we do not like as well even as the second. The officials of the Canadian company are endeavouring to get the commitments that would provide for the implementing of No. 1. They are also ascertaining whether, in the event that is not possible, they could get the the commitments that would be necessary for the implementation of No. 2. That is the situation. I hope we shall not have to fall back on No. 3.
The Prime Minister was questioned again by the hon. member for Prince Albert on July 12, two days ago. The answers he gave then were very illuminating. In the meantime there had been press dispatches to the effect that Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited might give a guarantee that within five years or within seven years they would build an all-Canadian line, or that they might not be able to give any undertaking unless there had been a market built up in southern Ontario and Quebec by means of United States gas. Here are the Prime Minister's answers to the questions two days ago. He dealt with a specific time limit within which the allCanadian line was to be built, and he said the financial houses would have to be satisfied, otherwise the line could not be financed. Then I asked him:
Has there been any change in the government policy announced in 1953 that the needs of the Canadian people for natural gas must be assured before there is any permission to export?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
There has been no change in the general policy. Consideration is being given to the kind of situation that had to be met with respect to providing gas for Vancouver. There, there had to be a pipe line that will have a capacity greater than the quantity of gas Vancouver can consume at this time, and so there has been an arrangement to allow the surplus that would be carried in the pipe line to be exported.
Nobody is complaining about that, either in regard to the west coast pipe line or the pipe line to eastern Canada, provided that pipe line is laid on Canadian soil. The Prime Minister went on:
Similar considerations may apply to a pipe line that would bring gas eastward. It may be that at this time it would have to have a greater capacity than the Canadian market in eastern Canada would now absorb. The question that is being discussed and about which negotiations are proceeding is to find what could be done with that surplus over and above eastern requirements at this time without making commitments that would not leave the gas available when the eastern Canadian market will have further developed.
The hon. member for Prince Albert then asked him a further question, and the Prime Minister said:
I cannot fix any specific date.
That is, any date by which the all-Canadian line would be completed.
I am satisfied that they are proceeding just as expeditiously as they can to secure the commitments that would be required to make the proposal one that financial houses would look upon with 50433-390J
Supply-Trade and Commerce favour. As I said a moment ago, it may be difficult to get a commitment that such and such will be done on such a date.
These are the key words:
We may have to be satisfied with a commitment that all efforts will be made to develop the market and that, when it reaches a certain quota, the commitment will then become an absolute obligation.
I do not think that is a very definite commitment, if that is all that is going to be required of this chosen instrument, Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited. It seems perfectly clear that these three schemes which are before the government are, first, a main line, all-Canadian, with a branch line to Minneapolis; second, the larger pipe line, allCanadian, with the excess sold to the eastern United States at Niagara. I believe that would serve northern Ontario and it would reduce the price of gas along the line because of the larger volume of gas carried, because of what they call the bigger through-put. It would be similar to the plan now in effect on the west coast, which is a pipe line from the Peace river portion of British Columbia and Alberta through central British Columbia, serving practically the whole of British Columbia except Vancouver island and possibly Vancouver island as well, with the excess going down into the northwestern states. This second plan would mean that the Canadian gas would be in Canadian hands all the way to Niagara and, of course, that all the gas needed in Canada would be kept under control of Canada at all times with the excess going to the United States.
The third plan, it is perfectly obvious from the Prime Minister's statement, is to export gas to the central states in large quantities; in other words, make that the main pipe line from Alberta and, presumably, not only to Minneapolis but to Chicago, and then down to Pennsylvania and throughout the Tennessee Gas Transmission Company system; and, on the other hand, to import United States gas for Ontario and Quebec.
That means, of course, that northern Ontario and the lakehead would be excluded. They will be out of luck for gas, certainly for five years, perhaps for seven, and probably for all time. The Prime Minister is hinting that the government will take some kind of guarantee from Trans-Canada Pipe Lines that when the southern Ontario and Quebec market has been built up, then they will construct the pipe line through northern Ontario. I can only point out to you, Mr. Chairman, and to the members from northern Ontario and from the lakehead-

speechtext:
Never mind about looking after northern Ontario. What about looking after British Columbia for a change?

speechtext: We have all read those proceedings. Is this another filibuster my hon. friend is putting on? It is a very poor show.
Answer the questions.

speechtext: He does not stop long enough. How can I answer questions when he is on his feet?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce

During the discussion in the committee last year I asked Mr. Schultz some questions. He was vice-president of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited. I am quoting from page 45. The hon. member for Calgary South had asked that question.

speechtext: You and the hon. member for Calgary South are a great pair.
The answer was as follows:

Well, our experts have never
claimed that we needed any help in doing this job. I would not contemplate that a project of such national importance should receive less treatment than the set-up which interprovincial or any other important project has received in the way of sales tax and duty remissions. But even without that I do not think that we have to have it, because I think that we can make it work; and it all goes back to what we have always said: That this project would have three rough years, and that as we got a market built up, the project would be entirely economic and go along by itself.
Again at page 66 I was questioning him and I asked this:
Do you believe that your original plan for a pipe line, without branches to the United States, would be an economic proposition? Mr. Schultz: Yes
You have not changed your mind about that?

Not since I was here three years ago.
Then the brokers were asked the same question or the representatives of the financial houses. Mr. Baldwin of Nesbitt, Thomson and Company Limited appeared before the committee and I asked him some questions.
I refer to page 81:
You have heard the discussion today. Could you tell the committee what you consider it is possible to do or not to do in connection with financing this project?

Obviously, we have followed this project from its early beginnings, feeling very definitely that one of the greatest responsibilities of the investment houses of Canada is to bend every effort to find the capital needed to develop our national resources. We have been very much intrigued with that. I will not attempt to say to you more than that my firm, the people we are associated with and I personally believe very strongly that the money can be raised on a favourable basis for this project.

Mr. Natelson representing the New York financial houses was also questioned, and he gave evidence much to the same effect. But now there seems to have been a reversal of policy by this company and I ask the minister why the field should not be open to other companies.
Mr. Chairman,-
Would the minister answer that question?

Just before he answers the question, Mr. Chairman, I should like to say that I have been surprised at the patience of the minister. This pipe line has been handled by the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, and it belongs to the Minister of Transport. I am surprised at the minister's patience. It is far greater than mine.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, my hon. friend started by reading a statement of policy stated by myself. He asked the Prime Minister if there was any change in that policy. The Prime Minister said no. Mr. Chairman,-
Mr. Chairman, is there any reason why-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

We have assured ourselves that the government is conscious of all of the things mentioned by the hon. member. Furthermore, we are convinced beyond a shadow of a doubt that the cabinet is also conscious of the great importance of an all-Canadian line if it can be constructed economically.

Supply-Trade and Commerce of the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian National Railways; and quite naturally it must take time. No snap judgments can be made. Will the minister tell the committee whether there have been any negotiations between the government of Canada and the government of the United States concerning any plan to export Alberta gas to the United States and import United States gas into Ontario and Quebec?

speechtext:
Take it any way
you like.

speechtext: I said, take it any way you like.
Mr. Chairman, that is a high mark in courtesy by the minister.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the resolution carry?
Carried.
No. I have some questions.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: On item 428 or item 429?
No. The first item is not carried.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall item 428 carry?
Carried.

I have some questions to ask. I did not know whether another hon. member wished to speak. I indicated some questions to the minister this afternoon. Will he deal, first of all, with the situation with regard to hardboard and the efforts in the United States to restrict imports thereof from Canada?

Supply-Trade and Commerce

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The position is that the bill introduced in their House of Representatives is, I believe, still in committee. Our representations have been made, and we are hopeful that there will be no change in the tariff on hardboard. But I cannot say more without attempting to forecast what congress will do in the future.
Will the minister bring us up to date on the matter of the measure before congress to simplify the United States customs administration?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I cannot say as to that. I believe it has been reported out of committee. Whether it will be dealt with at this session I cannot say. I believe it has been dealt with in the Senate, but not in the house. I cannot be positive. Anyway, it is in the legislative mill.

I have a general question on the picture for 1955 with regard to wheat exports. Comparing the figures for 1952, 1953 and 1954, I notice there has been a drop of about 40 per cent in the dollar value of Canadian exports of wheat. Flour exports are down about 22 per cent and barley about 40 per cent. What is the general picture for 1955?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Are we on the
wheat item? We finished the first item, did we not?
This is on the administration item.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I think we have carried administration.
No. My questions were on the first item. We are still on the first item.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Why not wait until we get to the wheat item?

I would be willing to let it go until then. I have a few questions with regard to bacon and beef. I see they are not included in the first 20 items of Canada's exports. I should like to know whether the minister can give a statement as to what the picture is with regard to being able to win back our bacon market in the United Kingdom, or our market for beef.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The position as to bacon is that we sell our surplus to the United States at very much better prices than we can get in the United Kingdom. If my hon. friend knows of any exporters on the prairies who would like to take the United Kingdom price we could easily arrange to export their bacon to the United Kingdom.
Is the same true of beef?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The same is true with regard to beef.

I have one question for the minister. I am not exactly sure whether it comes within his department, but he can tell me if it does not. It has to do with engineering, and I know he is very interested in that.
A great deal of the engineering work on a large part of our chemical and petrochemical industries is being done in the United States. I think the minister has received correspondence about this problem. Has he given any thought at all to any plan which would enable us to keep our engineers in Canada doing this work? I understand that over the last four years about $20 million has been spent on engineering work in the United States in this line alone. I know it is something you cannot protect by tariffs, but is any thought being given as to how we might keep these people in Canada on this type of job?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: As far as I know every engineer in Canada with a reputation has all the work he can handle, and most of our engineering firms are short of qualified men. I suppose the government is probably the largest employer of engineers in Canada. Engineers are picked up as they graduate from university and are given opportunities here that I think are quite equal to the opportunities they can obtain elsewhere. For occasional highly specialized work it is natural to go outside the country, because we have not the required type of experience in Canada, but I think where the type of experience is available in Canada the tendency of Canadian firms is to use Canadian engineers.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Trade commissioner service

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: 430.	Administration and operation, $2,855,438.

Can the minister tell us what instructions, if any, are given to the trade commissioners and others overseas with respect to the use or selling of the use of Canadian ports for the handling of exports and imports of goods?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Goods moving to or from commonwealth countries must pass through Canadian ports in order to get the preference. That is a must. The arrangements in Canada are that unless there is a specific instruction by the shipper the goods are to be moved through Canadian ports. If the railroad does not have definite instructions otherwise it is instructed to use Canadian ports. Our trade commissioners, as part

of their course of instruction, are told to stress the importance of Canadian ports and, as a matter of fact, the bulk of our goods does move through Canadian ports. It is quite a change since the early thirties, when not much attention was paid to that sort of thing.

With respect to the remark the minister has made, I think I should say I am not particularly finding fault with the fact that there has been some change since the thirties. I am simply saying that there is tremendous room for improvement in this respect, and I still think greater effort should be made by the department in this regard.

I should like to express my appreciation to the minister for the work this branch is doing in making available information regarding the port of Churchill. A year ago the governments of Saskatchewan and Manitoba produced a very interesting booklet telling about the possibilities of this new northern port. While our trade commissioners could not be expected to show any preference between Saint John, Halifax, or Montreal in advocating the use of Canadian ports, they have undertaken to display this valuable booklet in their overseas offices, and prospective shippers have access to copies of it. They are able to take advantage of the fact that shipping through Churchill to the prairie market does offer very real attractions. I should like to express my appreciation to the minister's department for the courtesy extended by the trade commissioners in Europe in making this booklet available to people who are exporting to this part of the world.

I want to ask the minister a question based on one or two sentences found on page 22 of the department's report for 1954, having to do with the Canadian trade commissioner service. Near the bottom of the page there is the following:
This branch must expand if it is to give continuing leadership in the extension of Canadian foreign trade and to render proper service as the eyes, ears, and sometimes the arms of Canadian business.
Later I read:
Constant attempts are being made to evaluate the trade possibilities of areas in which we are insufficiently represented; changes in world trade patterns may indicate the desirability and necessity of opening new offices . . .
Can the minister describe and illustrate to us the division of work and inquiry as between private enterprise, which is going to do the business eventually, and the department? In reading the details of the employment of the officers in the service, as set out on page 21, it would appear that they all seem to be employed in various specific
Supply-Trade and Commerce duties, and I should like to know more as to the method by which the leadership I referred to and the evaluation of trade possibilities in new areas is worked out in conjunction with private enterprise.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The trade commissioners are the people on the spot who act as the eyes and ears of Canadian business. A Canadian businessman going to a foreign country usually goes to the trade commissioner's office. There he is given the information he needs and the contacts he wishes to make are arranged. If he needs an interpreter that is arranged. Then when a trade commissioner returns to Canada he takes a tour across the country and visits the businessmen in every city to discuss trade possibilities in the area which he represents. I must say that it is rather unusual for a businessman to go abroad on a business trip without writing me on his return to Canada to extend special thanks to the trade commissioners who have made his business arrangements easy to develop.

I think the minister has covered my question fully in respect of places where we now have trade commissioners. It seemed to me this implied that the department was reaching out beyond and exploring new areas. It was that particularly I wanted to ask him about.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes, the evaluation work is headquarters work based on reports from the field. Returning businessmen come in and say what they need in the field. In other words, if they believe an area is not properly served they report that to headquarters. Last year we opened two new posts, one in Salisbury and the other in Copenhagen. This coming year we are asking that funds be provided to open four new offices. A good many factors have to be taken into account before the actual decision is arrived at, but we have certain points in mind that we believe warrant trade offices. It is quite probable that the locations presently in mind will be those finally chosen, although we are not too sure.

I wish to repeat at this point something I said on this item in a previous session. It is by way of paying tribute to the quality of the men engaged in the trade commissioner service. The Department of Trade and Commerce, I believe, is one of the most fortunate of all departments in the senior officials it has in the department. The trade commissioner service is one of the government services that is manned by the best Canadians we have anywhere in our public service.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
I made mention of this on a previous occasion, based on contacts I had had with a number of trade commissioners in travels abroad up to that time. It happened that last summer several members of this house had occasion to travel through Africa after the commonwealth parliamentary conference at Nairobi in Kenya. Some of us met the Canadian trade commissioners at Capetown, Johannesburg and Cairo. There again one's impression of the quality of these men and the service they render was confirmed. I just wish to pay that tribute because these men are a long way from home. Sometimes they are in association with the Canadian diplomatic representatives and sometimes they are completely on their own. But from my observations I think-and I have now had the pleasure of seeing quite a number of them-they are very worthy representatives of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I should like to thank my hon. friend for that tribute. It is confirmed by my own impression gathered from travels about various parts of the world. Our men are very carefully selected graduates of universities. They are given a special course of training and then sent on tour before they are sent to the field. We believe they should have a thorough knowledge of Canadian business requirements before they go abroad. They are put under an experienced trade commissioner, and graduate from there into posts of their own.
I think it is a splendid service. I believe we are particularly fortunate in the younger men, and the older men as well, we have in the field. That is confirmed almost every week by letters from Canadians who have travelled abroad on business.

There is one point of detail about which I should like to ask a question. As is natural, in most cases one finds the staff is either the same as it was before or higher. I notice that in Paris the staff is down three and also the expenses are down considerably. I wonder if that is just a rub of the green or whether there is some change in the business situation.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: We found there were so many restrictions on both exports to France and imports from France that prudence would indicate we did not require as large a staff there as we had had previously and therefore men were transferred to other posts. However, we have a very experienced trade commissioner in Paris, and he has a staff that we believe is adequate for the present.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.

Trade commissioner service-
431.	Acquisition or improvement of buildings, land, equipment, and furnishings, $100,000.

The particulars of this item of $100,000 on page 524 indicate that there is one item of $85,000 for the acquisition or improvement of buildings and land and another item of $15,000 for the acquisition of equipment, furniture and furnishings for residences abroad. Would the minister indicate just where the posts are at which those expenditures are to be made?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes. We have found it necessary to buy a house for our trade commissioner at Kingston, Jamaica. There was absolutely no accommodation available, and the money we asked for will be sufficient to provide accommodation for one or two other posts where it is impossible to rent suitable accommodation.
What is the breakdown of the amounts?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Madrid, Kingston, Leopoldville, Tokyo and Karachi.
Could we have the amounts in each place?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The amounts here are Madrid, $35,000; Kingston, Jamaica, $30,000; Leopoldville, $40,000; Tokyo, $40,000; Karachi, $35,000.
You are over the $100,000 now.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes, but we do not expect to finish this program in one year.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
432.	Information branch. $211,209.

This is the item for the information branch. In the detail on page 525, the fifth item from the end, there is an item for advertising in Canada and abroad which is to be increased from $28,000 last year to $78,000 this year. What is that for, and what accounts for this large increase?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: We are starting in again to advertise cheese in the United Kingdom. We have been slowly building a quality market for cheese there, and we believe that it is sufficiently developed now to warrant a real advertising campaign. We are also advertising flour and timber in the United Kingdom.
Do I understand the $78,000 is all to be expended in the United Kingdom?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Advertising in the United Kingdom, under the direction of the commercial counsellor, London, England, $15,000 as against $6,500 last year; advertising in directories, annuals and Canadian export

papers, etc., $4,500 as against $7,500 last year. The Canadian advertising is reduced. Advertising in special editions and supplementaries is also reduced from $6,000 to $4,000. Production and mechanical charges, $4,000, the same as last year; special promotional campaigns, $50,000. As I said this $50,000 is all for the United Kingdom. It is to be devoted to advertising in the United Kingdom of Canadian cheese, Canadian timber and Canadian flour.

Would that have anything to do with the resale of our recent import of
2,250,000	pounds of cheese from New Zealand?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That is a different quality cheese. That type of cheese is not available in Canada, and is not competitive with Canadian cheese. It was a small import of a special quality cheese.

I should like to ask the minister a question in connection with this item, as it refers to Colombo plan disbursements. As a member of parliament I find it difficult to get information regarding problems being encountered. What is being done? I understand Canada is doing something. Mr. C a veil has done a good job. But it is difficult to find out whether the Department of External Affairs, the Department of Agriculture or the minister's department is taking the responsibility for public information in these fields.
Would the minister indicate whether his department does take the responsibility for giving the Canadian people information regarding the job being done by those who are working on the plan. Would he also give information regarding the personnel who come to Canada for work in connection with our Colombo plan disbursements.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Responsibility for the administration of Colombo plan funds is that of the Department of Trade and Commerce. We will be reaching item 448, and could have the discussion at that time.

My complaint is that that branch does not seem to have any information service. I suggest that at some point in the minister's department there should be an appropriation for information. During the war the minister had a very efficient information service to inform the Canadian people as to what was being done in the field of munitions and supply. If he is spending $26 million abroad, it appears to me more money should be spent in the field of information. I do not think it is possible under this item for $211,209 to do the sort of thing that ought to be done; and the
Supply-Trade and Commerce $26 million does not make provision for the dispersal of public information.
What money is being spent in the field? The minister should give consideration to having a fund set up either in his department or in the Department of External Affairs to deal with the problem of pubic information.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The information branch of the Department of Trade and Commerce co-operates with the information branch of the Department of External Affairs in handling matters of that kind. The Department of External Affairs has the responsibility for deciding the amount to be spent on various projects, and the administration is carried out by the Department of Trade and Commerce. Information is put out sometimes by one department and sometimes by the other. But we do not boast too much about our Colombo plan efforts.

That is an important point. My whole criticism is that when I ask the Department of External Affairs for information in connection with a problem being undertaken, and how we are spending the $26 million, they just pass the buck to the Department of Trade and Commerce. The Department of Trade and Commerce, in turn, is short-staffed. They have sent me some information, but they do not pretend to have the staff available to do a worth-while job in the field of public information. If we are going to spend $26 million we should spend enough to tell whether it is a worth-while project or not, and what is being done.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The Department of Trade and Commerce is not primarily a propaganda department. However, I will give consideration to strengthening our public information service, with the thought that we might give more information concerning work connected with the Colombo plan.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
433.	Economics branch. $234,265.
Mr. Pallet!: I note that the expenditure this year is $59,387 greater than it was last year. Some economists have been added to the staff. Would the minister state what extra service is being rendered for the extra money he asks to have voted.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
The history of this branch is that back in 1947, I believe it was, the Department of Trade and Commerce took over the work of the department of munitions and supply, and of the department of reconstruction. At that time we took over the economics branch of those departments. Certain engineering work was to be cleared up. It is a small branch but it has been a very useful one, particularly on projects such
8170	HOUSE OF
Supply-Trade and Commerce as pipe lines or projects requiring a combination of engineering and economics to make a proper study.
Mr. Pallet!: Is any work done as a result of private submissions to the branch? If a company were interested in a large private project, could information be obtained from the department through this branch as to the economic merits or otherwise of such project?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Any information available in the branch could be made available in connection with a private project. We are not consulting engineers, but the purpose of the department is to be of service to Canadian business and any service the department can render is rendered gladly to Canadian businessmen.
Do I understand the minister to say that the economics branch, and the 20 economists shown in the list, originally was a legacy from the department of munitions and supply?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes, and also taken over from the department of reconstruction.

I have one further question. I observe in the telephone directory that the economics branch is divided into economic forecasting and general analysis, under which ten names are listed, and also under the heading of industry analysis. What is the relationship between the economists shown in this department and those in the dominion bureau of statistics? Are there economists there, too.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
There are no
economists in the bureau of statistics; they are statisticians. Their work is that of collecting information and making it available to anyone desiring it. The purpose of the staff in the Department of Trade and Commerce is to make an analysis of that information, and to issue forecasts based upon information gathered by the bureau of statistics and through economic surveys. We think we have the strongest economic staff in the Dominion of Canada; I think so, anyway.
I would not argue with the minister on that. But are there no economists as such in the bureau of statistics? Would the bureau of statistics admit there are no economists there?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
The bureau has people with economics training but they are employed as statisticians. The bureau of statistics is not encouraged to do forecasting,


or to do other than present facts as disclosed to them by figures they collect.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Exhibitions-
435.	Exhibitions generally, $313,590.

In the details at page 528, after listing a number of individual trade fairs, there is an omnibus item for participation in other exhibitions, and there is an increase from $78,000 to $98,500. Could we have an explanation of the increase?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I think the answer is that having given up the international trade fair, the purpose is to do more and better work at exhibitions abroad. We think it is more productive so far as Canadian business is concerned. This item covers the exhibition at Berlin; we were in that last year. The amount is the same, $17,500. Hanover, $15,000, the same as last year; the French trade fair, $17,000, the same as last year; the Kansas City fair, $3,500, the same as last year; Japanese trade fair at Tokyo, $6,500, up from $5,000; United Kingdom exhibit, $22,000. That is a new item. Agricultural products show in the United Kingdom; we dropped that in favour of the United Kingdom exhibit. Then there is an "unforeseen" item which is the same as last year, $17,000. That is to enable the government to accept other invitations to participate in fairs if it is thought worth while.
Does that make up the total of $98,500?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes.

There is one comment I should like to make on the subject of exhibits generally. I think all hon. members recognize that these trade fairs abroad do give an opportunity for the department to make Canada's products known. It is important that they be Canada's products. There is one fair abroad at which a number of fur garments were being exhibited in the Canadian space which, I am told on good authority, included a number of American garments.
I had occasion to say something about this.
I believe since that occasion some Canadian garments have been sent over there. These are all fur garments.
I raise this point now because I think it is so important that when Canada is taking advantage of the opportunity of sending exhibits to those trade fairs abroad we make very sure that these are strictly Canadian products that are being exhibited. I think

steps have since been taken to make sure that the garments exhibited were strictly Canadian products, but originally some of those exhibitors, who were asked to contribute fur garments to the exhibit, sent along some American imports and some French styles as well, apparently on the theory that European styles would have more appeal to Europeans at European trade fairs. I do not think that is the principal purpose. Rather the principal purpose of these exhibits, as I understand it, is to make Canada's wares known abroad.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, that is quite correct. However, I doubt whether there was an exhibit of American furs. I refer particularly to the fair at Brussels, where Canada has had the most spectacular exhibit both of furs and of textiles. As far as I know all the furs and textiles in that exhibit were Canadian. The catalogue was beautifully gotten up. I think it was partly paid for by the trade and partly by the department. The exhibit was moved on to other European cities later on. I am told that the results were rather spectacular as far as the sales of Canadian furs are concerned.

I am in a position to tell the minister that in the original exhibit some garments of American manufacture and also French styles were included in the exhibit. Part of the exhibit at least was contributed by the trade; but when the matter was raised-I happen to know the occasion; it was about two months ago-steps were taken to put Canadian-made garments in their place. I raise it now because I am quite sure the minister was not aware of it. I am sure there is no wish in the department to see garments other than of strictly Canadian manufacture included in the Canadian exhibits in these trade fairs abroad.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The purpose of the exhibit of course is to help the Canadian fur trade. We arranged the facilities and the trade furnished the garments and the models, the exhibits generally. We shared in the cost of the catalogue and the exhibit space. It is possible, of course, that some of the Canadian exhibitors brought in foreign furs. That would be without the knowledge of the department. I must say that it looked very beautiful. I am not enough of a connoisseur to know which was Canadian and which was not.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Supply-Trade and Commerce
436.	Canadian participation in the Brussels universal and international exhibition 1958-preparatory expenses, $50,000.

At the bottom of page 528 there is an item as follows:
Brussels universal and international exhibition 1953-preparatory expenses.
Participation in Brussels universal and international exhibition, $50,000.
Is it necessary to set up $50,000 preparatory expenses three years in advance of this exhibition?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
The Brussels fair is a great world fair. We think there is no time to spare in getting the Canadian building up and the Canadian exhibit organized. I believe our appropriation for the fair is something over $2 million. We are actively at work in preparation for it today. The Brussels world's fair is going to be the biggest thing that has been held in Europe since the war. We think it important that Canada be well placed in the exhibit.
437.	Canadian international trade fair-to provide for the net operating deficit during the current fiscal year of the special operating account in the consolidated revenue fund; advances to be made to the account as required, but not to exceed in the aggregate, $275,000.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to speak very strongly on behalf of continuing the international trade fair. I have some figures here which I would be glad to give to the minister, but I am sure he has the same figures. I have here a list of 48 foreign firms which exhibited at the trade fair between 1948 and 1953, which either have established or are in the process of establishing branch plants in Canada to manufacture their products in this country. There is no doubt about it that the great majority, if not all, of these firms learned of the potential Canadian market by first of all exhibiting their goods at this trade fair. There the potential buyers sampled these goods and decided whether they liked them and placed orders. If it had not been for that the firms certainly would never have thought of setting up branch plants here in Canada.
The establishment of 48 individual branch factories to produce goods in this country, which otherwise in all likelihood never would have been established here, is a very good advertisement for this trade fair. That in itself far more that justifies its continuance.
If 48 firms could be established through the fact that these firms were able to exhibit during six years, the indication is that more and more firms would be inclined to do the same thing if this fair were continued and additional foreign firms were able to come
6172	HOUSE OF
Supply-Trade and Commerce here to exhibit their wares, to find out what the market was in Canada for their goods. I should like to hear what the minister has to say about the possibility of this international trade fair being continued, and whether he has definitely decided to discontinue it. If so, will he give us the reasons for so doing.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I gave a complete statement on the subject on Wednesday, June 8, at page 4530 of Hansard. Briefly, we felt that the trade fair has served its purpose. It was instituted immediately after the war to offer an opportunity for firms in other countries such as England, France and Belgium to establish their goods in the Canadian market, and also to examine the business opportunities in Canada.
I think the fair was a success from the start, though there was one year when there seemed to be some slipping away. I believe last year was also a successful year. I attended it. I think it was very well conducted; but it was quite obvious that some of the customers who had made the fair successful at first were no longer with us. The British exhibit was much smaller. There were a greater number of prestige exhibits from such countries as Czechoslovakia and other European countries that were never big traders in this market. There was also a falling off in the exhibits by Canadian firms.
I may say that some effort was exerted 'to get the larger Canadian firms to exhibit. I felt many of them were doing it reluctantly. It is the view of my officers, in which I concur, that it is better to wind up the fair when it is a success than carry it on for a year or two and wind it up as a failure. That is the decision that has been taken, and that decision cannot be changed. There is an item of $100,000 to clean up the accounts of the fair, and that will be the last appearance of any item for the international trade fair.

Mr. Chairman,
I think there have been statements made about placing the facilities which have been accumulated by the government in connection with the fair at the disposal of either the municipality of metropolitan Toronto or the provincial government. I wonder if the minister might confirm that some such arrangement as that might be made, if either of those two authorities wished to carry on this fair.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes, I made that offer in the house. If either authority wishes to carry it on we shall be glad to turn the appurtenances over to them.

Would the minister answer just one more question. Did he 

receive any representations by any groups of people at all to have the fair discontinued?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: No, there were no formal representations. I talked with a number of individuals, and my officers did the same. A thorough survey was made of Canadian business before we reached the decision. The decision was arrived at as a result of conferences with a great number of individuals. We have had no official representations from any organized body.

In connection with the minister's undertaking about the physical facilities, is there a chance that the services of some of the people who have been formerly employed full time on this project may be made available to the other authorities who might carry this on, or will they be discontinued completely by the dominion government?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: No, the senior officers who operated the trade fair are officers of the government in the exhibitions branch. Their services will be used in trade fairs elsewhere, perhaps some at the world's fair at Brussels and others at various exhibitions throughout the world.
Would their technical assistance still be available to either the province or the municipality that is prepared to carry on?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I would not like to make any decision on a question of that sort. If a specific case were put up we would try to be helpful. I would not like to promise at this time any particular help.

Mr. Chairman, would the minister tell us this? Are the items in the estimates for 1955-56 in respect of the trade fair just completed, which ran from the end of May to the 10th of June; or are they in respect of a trade fair which might have been contemplated at the time of the preparation of the estimates, to be held in 1956?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: These items cover everything that takes place in the current fiscal year, from the 1st of April this year to 31st of March next year. As the fair was held in that period, the cost of the fair is probably included.

The
point I have in mind is that perhaps the minister might want to give some consideration to some reduction in certain of these amounts. I am not attempting to argue here that I am at all pleased to see the end of the Canadian international trade fair, because I am not. If the government, as the minister

has indicated, has made that decision, then I think they should approach this particular situation from the viewpoint of sound business people.
When we look at this statement which we have in front of us, we find that in the period 1954-55, when presumably the trade fair was looked upon as being on a continuing basis and the staff would be kept at a constant level, they provided $138,000 in the form of salaries. In the current year, when presumably the trade fair is beginning to drop off to nothing and the staff is being steadily reduced, the estimates show $134,000. When we come down to the other expenditures in connection with the trade fair we find such things as travelling expenses, which were $26,800 in 1954-55, almost the same at $23,200. We find $55,000 in both years for publications. We find $177,000 last year and $182,000 this year for promotional activities, and so on right down the list.
I suggest it must be obvious that the trade fair of this year now being over, and there being no anticipated trade fair for next year, one would expect some sizeable reductions in these expenditures. I should be grateful if the minister would indicate to the house what it is proposed to do about this, because it is hardly right that he should come here and ask for sizeable sums of money which he has no intention of using.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, my hon. friend is quite correct. These estimates were prepared early in the year and included the usual expenditures for the international trade fair. The decision to drop the fair was taken on the 8th of June. The money will not all be used this year, but until we get the fair liquidated it is difficult to know just how much we shall require. Of course there will be some considerable revenue from the fair, which will go directly to the receiver general, but there will probably be quite a large unexpended balance of this amount owing to the fact that the fair is not being held next year.
have another question, Mr. Chairman. Have we not $100,000 in the supplementary estimates in connection with the Canadian international trade fair?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: No, I understand that there is no item. I mentioned $100,000 as being the amount that is likely to be spent in cleaning up this account, which probably is the item we would have put in had we known the fair was going to close.

In
the interest of a sound approach to government business, has the minister considered reducing his requests in the estimates for
Supply-Trade and Commerce the Canadian international trade fair? I do not know how the minister feels about it, but it gives me pause to be asked to approve estimates when I know, and have the word of the minister as well, that it is not intended to use the money.

It can be used only for a specific purpose, for the Canadian international trade fair. No one knows just how much will be required to liquidate the fair.

You
just said $100,000.

speechtext: That was my guess. I do not know whether that is right or not; it is out of the air. Since this is the last time the item will appear I think it might as well go through as is.
